questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: The amount of charge passing through a cross-section of a wire in time $t$ is given by $Q(t) = At^2 + Bt + C$. Determine the dimensional formulae for $A$, $B$, and $C$.
questions.solution:
According to the principle of homogeneity of dimensions, each term in the expression $At^2 + Bt + C$ must have the same dimensional formula as the charge $Q$.

The dimensional formula of charge $Q$ is $[IT]$.

For the first term:
$[At^2] = [Q]$
$[A][T^2] = [IT]$
$[A] = [IT^{-1}]$

For the second term:
$[Bt] = [Q]$
$[B][T] = [IT]$
$[B] = [I]$

For the third term:
$[C] = [Q]$
$[C] = [IT]$

Thus, the dimensional formulae for $A$, $B$, and $C$ are $IT^{-1}$, $I$, and $IT$ respectively.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A discharge tube carries an electric current of $2.0 \mu\text{A}$. Determine the amount of charge that passes through a cross-section of the tube in $5$ minutes.
questions.solution:
Given current $I = 2.0 \mu\text{A} = 2.0 \times 10^{-6} \text{ A}$

Time $t = 5 \text{ minutes} = 5 \times 60 \text{ s} = 300 \text{ s}$

The amount of charge $Q$ passing through a cross-section is given by the relation $Q = I \times t$

Substituting the values:

$Q = 2.0 \times 10^{-6} \times 300$

$Q = 600 \times 10^{-6} \text{ C}$

$Q = 6.0 \times 10^{-4} \text{ C}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: The current flowing through a wire varies with time according to $i = i_0 + \alpha t$, where $i_0 = 10 \text{ A}$ and $\alpha = 4 \text{ A s}^{-1}$. Determine the charge that crosses a section of the wire in $10$ seconds.
questions.solution:
The current flowing through the wire is given by $i = \dfrac{dq}{dt} = i_0 + \alpha t$

The charge $q$ crossing a section of the wire in time $t$ is obtained by integrating the current:

$q = \int_{0}^{t} i \, dt$

Substituting the given values $i_0 = 10 \text{ A}$ and $\alpha = 4 \text{ A s}^{-1}$:

$q = \int_{0}^{10} (10 + 4t) \, dt$

$q = \left[ 10t + \dfrac{4t^2}{2} \right]_{0}^{10}$

$q = \left[ 10t + 2t^2 \right]_{0}^{10}$

$q = 10(10) + 2(10)^2$

$q = 100 + 200 = 300 \text{ C}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A copper wire with a cross-section of $1.0 \text{ mm}^2$ carries a current of $1.0 \text{ A}$. Determine the drift speed of the free electrons in the wire, assuming there is one free electron per atom. The density of copper is $9000 \text{ kg m}^{-3}$.
questions.solution:
The number density of free electrons is equal to the number density of copper atoms, given by:

$n = \dfrac{N_A d}{M}$

Substituting the standard values for copper ($N_A \approx 6.02 \times 10^{23} \text{ mol}^{-1}$, $M \approx 63.5 \text{ g mol}^{-1} = 63.5 \times 10^{-3} \text{ kg mol}^{-1}$):

$n = \dfrac{6.02 \times 10^{23} \times 9000}{63.5 \times 10^{-3}} \approx 8.5 \times 10^{28} \text{ m}^{-3}$

The drift speed $v_d$ is given by the relation:

$I = n e A v_d$

Rearranging for $v_d$:

$v_d = \dfrac{I}{n e A}$

Substituting the given values ($I = 1.0 \text{ A}$, $e = 1.6 \times 10^{-19} \text{ C}$, $A = 1.0 \times 10^{-6} \text{ m}^2$):

$v_d = \dfrac{1.0}{8.5 \times 10^{28} \times 1.6 \times 10^{-19} \times 1.0 \times 10^{-6}}$

$v_d \approx \dfrac{1.0}{13.6 \times 10^3} \text{ m s}^{-1} \approx 0.074 \times 10^{-3} \text{ m s}^{-1}$

$v_d = 0.074 \text{ mm s}^{-1}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: An electron gun releases $2.0 \times 10^{16}$ electrons per second. Determine the electric current this corresponds to.
questions.solution:
Electric current is defined as the rate of flow of electric charge.

$I = \dfrac{q}{t}$

Since $q = ne$, where $n$ is the number of electrons and $e$ is the elementary charge, the current can be written as:

$I = \dfrac{n}{t} \times e$

Given the number of electrons released per second is $\dfrac{n}{t} = 2.0 \times 10^{16} \text{ s}^{-1}$ and the charge of an electron is $e = 1.6 \times 10^{-19} \text{ C}$.

$I = (2.0 \times 10^{16}) \times (1.6 \times 10^{-19}) \text{ A}$

$I = 3.2 \times 10^{-3} \text{ A}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: The amount of charge passing through a cross-section of a wire in time $t$ is $Q(t) = At^2 + Bt + C$. Assuming the numerical values of $A$, $B$, and $C$ in SI units are $5$, $3$, and $1$ respectively, find the value of the current at $t = 5 \text{ s}$.
questions.solution:
Given the charge passing through the cross-section as a function of time:

$Q(t) = At^2 + Bt + C$

The current $I$ is the rate of flow of charge, given by the derivative of $Q(t)$ with respect to time $t$:

$I(t) = \dfrac{dQ}{dt} = \dfrac{d}{dt}(At^2 + Bt + C) = 2At + B$

Substituting the given numerical values $A = 5$ and $B = 3$:

$I(t) = 2(5)t + 3 = 10t + 3$

At $t = 5 \text{ s}$, the current is:

$I(5) = 10(5) + 3 = 50 + 3 = 53 \text{ A}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A uniform wire having a resistance of $100 \Omega$ is melted and recast into a new wire whose length is double that of the original. What will be the resistance of the new wire?
questions.solution:
Let the original resistance be $R_1 = 100 \Omega$, original length be $L_1$, and original area of cross-section be $A_1$.

The resistance of the original wire is given by $R_1 = \rho \dfrac{L_1}{A_1}$.

When the wire is melted and recast, its volume remains constant. Thus, $V = L_1 A_1 = L_2 A_2$.

Given that the new length is $L_2 = 2 L_1$.

The new area of cross-section is $A_2 = \dfrac{V}{L_2} = \dfrac{L_1 A_1}{2 L_1} = \dfrac{A_1}{2}$.

The resistance of the new wire is $R_2 = \rho \dfrac{L_2}{A_2} = \rho \dfrac{2 L_1}{\dfrac{A_1}{2}} = 4 \rho \dfrac{L_1}{A_1}$.

Therefore, $R_2 = 4 R_1 = 4 \times 100 = 400 \Omega$.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: Determine the required length of a copper wire having a cross-sectional area of $0.01 \text{ mm}^2$ to produce a resistance of $1 \text{ k}\Omega$. The resistivity of copper is given as $1.7 \times 10^{-8} \Omega \text{ m}$.
questions.solution:
The resistance of a wire is given by the formula:

$R = \rho \dfrac{l}{A}$

Rearranging for length $l$:

$l = \dfrac{R A}{\rho}$

Given values are:
$R = 1 \text{ k}\Omega = 10^3 \Omega$
$A = 0.01 \text{ mm}^2 = 0.01 \times 10^{-6} \text{ m}^2 = 10^{-8} \text{ m}^2$
$\rho = 1.7 \times 10^{-8} \Omega \text{ m}$

Substituting the values into the formula:

$l = \dfrac{10^3 \times 10^{-8}}{1.7 \times 10^{-8}}$

$l = \dfrac{1000}{1.7} \text{ m}$

$l \approx 588.2 \text{ m}$

$l \approx 0.588 \text{ km} \approx 0.59 \text{ km}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A wire with a length of $1 \text{ m}$ and a radius of $0.1 \text{ mm}$ possesses a resistance of $100 \Omega$. Determine the resistivity of the material.
questions.solution:
Given, length of the wire, $l = 1 \text{ m}$

Radius of the wire, $r = 0.1 \text{ mm} = 10^{-4} \text{ m}$

Resistance of the wire, $R = 100 \Omega$

The cross-sectional area of the wire is $A = \pi r^2 = \pi (10^{-4})^2 = \pi \times 10^{-8} \text{ m}^2$

Using the formula for resistance, $R = \rho \dfrac{l}{A}$

The resistivity of the material is $\rho = \dfrac{R A}{l}$

Substituting the given values, we get $\rho = \dfrac{100 \times \pi \times 10^{-8}}{1} = \pi \times 10^{-6} \Omega \text{ m}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A wire of length $4 \text{ m}$ and cross-sectional area $1 \text{ mm}^2$ carries a current of $2 \text{ A}$. Given that the material holds $10^{29}$ free electrons per cubic metre, determine the average time required for an electron to traverse the entire length of the wire.
questions.solution:
The drift velocity of free electrons is given by the relation $I = n e A v_d$, which gives $v_d = \dfrac{I}{n e A}$.

The average time required for an electron to traverse the length $L$ of the wire is $t = \dfrac{L}{v_d} = \dfrac{L n e A}{I}$.

Substituting the given values:
$L = 4 \text{ m}$
$n = 10^{29} \text{ m}^{-3}$
$e = 1.6 \times 10^{-19} \text{ C}$
$A = 1 \text{ mm}^2 = 10^{-6} \text{ m}^2$
$I = 2 \text{ A}$

$t = \dfrac{4 \times 10^{29} \times 1.6 \times 10^{-19} \times 10^{-6}}{2}$

$t = \dfrac{6.4 \times 10^4}{2}$

$t = 3.2 \times 10^4 \text{ s}$

questions.q: Consider a conductor of length $l$ with a circular cross section, as depicted in the figure. The cross-sectional radius changes linearly from $a$ to $b$. The material has a resistivity of $ ho$. Given that $b - a \ll l$, determine the resistance of the conductor.
questions.solution:
Consider an elemental disc of thickness $dx$ at a distance $x$ from the end with radius $a$.

The radius of this disc is given by $r = a + \dfrac{b-a}{l}x$.

The resistance of this elemental disc is $dR = \dfrac{\rho dx}{\pi r^2}$.

The total resistance of the conductor is obtained by integrating $dR$ from $x = 0$ to $x = l$:

$R = \int_{0}^{l} \dfrac{\rho dx}{\pi \left(a + \dfrac{b-a}{l}x\right)^2}$

Let $y = a + \dfrac{b-a}{l}x$. Then $dy = \dfrac{b-a}{l}dx$.

When $x = 0$, $y = a$, and when $x = l$, $y = b$.

Substituting these into the integral:

$R = \dfrac{\rho l}{\pi (b-a)} \int_{a}^{b} y^{-2} dy$

$R = \dfrac{\rho l}{\pi (b-a)} \left[ -\dfrac{1}{y} \right]_{a}^{b}$

$R = \dfrac{\rho l}{\pi (b-a)} \left( \dfrac{1}{a} - \dfrac{1}{b} \right)$

$R = \dfrac{\rho l}{\pi (b-a)} \left( \dfrac{b-a}{ab} \right)$

$R = \dfrac{\rho l}{\pi a b}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A power supply of $20 \text{ V}$ is connected across a copper wire having a resistance of $1 \text{ k}\Omega$ and a radius of $0.1 \text{ mm}$. Determine the number of electrons transferred per second between the supply and the wire at one of its ends.
questions.solution:
Given $V = 20 \text{ V}$ and $R = 1 \text{ k}\Omega = 1000 \Omega$.

The current flowing through the wire is given by Ohm's law:

$I = \dfrac{V}{R} = \dfrac{20}{1000} = 0.02 \text{ A}$

The current represents the rate of flow of charge, so the charge transferred per second is $q = 0.02 \text{ C}$.

The number of electrons transferred per second is:

$n = \dfrac{q}{e} = \dfrac{0.02}{1.6 \times 10^{-19}}$

$n = 1.25 \times 10^{17}$

The radius of the wire is extraneous information not required for this calculation.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A copper wire with a radius of $0.1 \text{ mm}$ and a resistance of $1 \text{ k}\Omega$ is connected across a $20 \text{ V}$ power supply. Determine the current density in the wire.
questions.solution:
Given, radius of the wire, $r = 0.1 \text{ mm} = 10^{-4} \text{ m}$

Resistance of the wire, $R = 1 \text{ k}\Omega = 10^3 \Omega$

Voltage across the wire, $V = 20 \text{ V}$

Current in the wire is given by Ohm's law:

$I = \dfrac{V}{R} = \dfrac{20}{10^3} = 2 \times 10^{-2} \text{ A}$

Cross-sectional area of the wire:

$A = \pi r^2 = \pi (10^{-4})^2 = \pi \times 10^{-8} \text{ m}^2$

Current density $J$ is the current per unit area:

$J = \dfrac{I}{A} = \dfrac{2 \times 10^{-2}}{\pi \times 10^{-8}} = \dfrac{2}{\pi} \times 10^6 \text{ A/m}^2$

$J \approx \dfrac{2}{3.1416} \times 10^6 \approx 0.6366 \times 10^6 \text{ A/m}^2 = 6.37 \times 10^5 \text{ A/m}^2$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: Determine the electric field within a copper wire that has a cross-sectional area of $2.0 \text{ mm}^2$ and carries a current of $1 \text{ A}$. The resistivity of copper is $1.7 \times 10^{-8} \Omega \text{ m}$.
questions.solution:
Given, cross-sectional area $A = 2.0 \text{ mm}^2 = 2.0 \times 10^{-6} \text{ m}^2$
Current $I = 1 \text{ A}$
Resistivity $\rho = 1.7 \times 10^{-8} \Omega \text{ m}$

Using the relation between electric field, resistivity, and current density:
$E = \rho J$

Since $J = \dfrac{I}{A}$, we have:
$E = \rho $\$left(\dfrac{I}{A}\right)

Substituting the given values:
$E = $\dfrac{1.7 \times 10^{-8} \times 1}{2.0 \times 10^{-6}}

$E = 0.85 \times 10^{-2} \text{ V/m}$

$E = 0.0085 \text{ V/m}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A wire of length $2.0 \text{ m}$ has a resistance of $5.0 \Omega$. Determine the electric field present inside the wire when a current of $10 \text{ A}$ flows through it.
questions.solution:
The potential difference $V$ across the wire is given by Ohm's law:

$V = IR$

Substituting the given values:

$V = 10 \times 5.0 = 50 \text{ V}$

The electric field $E$ inside a uniform wire of length $L$ is given by:

$E = \dfrac{V}{L}$

Substituting the values of $V$ and $L$:

$E = \dfrac{50}{2.0} = 25 \text{ V/m}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: At $20^{}^{{}^{\circ}} \text{C}$, an iron wire and a copper wire have resistances of $3.9 \Omega$ and $4.1 \Omega$, respectively. Determine the temperature at which their resistances become equal. The temperature coefficient of resistivity is $5.0 \times 10^{-3} \text{ K}^{-1}$ for iron and $4.0 \times 10^{-3} \text{ K}^{-1}$ for copper. Ignore any effects of thermal expansion.
questions.solution:
Let the initial temperature be $T_0 = 20^{}^{{}^{\circ}} \text{C}$ and the final temperature be $T$.

The resistance of a wire at temperature $T$ is given by $R = R_0[1 + \alpha(T - T_0)]$.

For the iron wire:
$R_{Fe} = 3.9 [1 + 5.0 \times 10^{-3} (T - 20)]$

For the copper wire:
$R_{Cu} = 4.1 [1 + 4.0 \times 10^{-3} (T - 20)]$

Equating the two resistances:
$3.9 [1 + 5.0 \times 10^{-3} (T - 20)] = 4.1 [1 + 4.0 \times 10^{-3} (T - 20)]$

$3.9 + 19.5 \times 10^{-3} (T - 20) = 4.1 + 16.4 \times 10^{-3} (T - 20)$

$(19.5 - 16.4) \times 10^{-3} (T - 20) = 4.1 - 3.9$

$3.1 \times 10^{-3} (T - 20) = 0.2$

$T - 20 = \dfrac{0.2}{3.1 \times 10^{-3}} = \dfrac{200}{3.1} \approx 64.5^{}^{{}^{\circ}} \text{C}$

$T = 20 + 64.5 = 84.5^{}^{{}^{\circ}} \text{C}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: An ammeter and a voltmeter are used to measure the current in a conductor and the potential difference across its terminals. Both meters draw negligible currents. The ammeter is perfectly accurate, whereas the voltmeter possesses a zero error (meaning it fails to read zero when no potential difference is present). Determine the zero error if the readings under two distinct conditions are $1.75 \text{ A}$, $14.4 \text{ V}$ and $2.75 \text{ A}$, $22.4 \text{ V}$.
questions.solution:
Let $R$ be the resistance of the conductor and $e$ be the zero error of the voltmeter.

The true potential difference across the conductor is given by Ohm's law as $V = IR$.

The voltmeter reading is $V' = V + e = IR + e$.

Using the given readings, we can write two equations:

$14.4 = 1.75 R + e$

$22.4 = 2.75 R + e$

Subtracting the first equation from the second yields:

$22.4 - 14.4 = (2.75 - 1.75) R$

$8.0 = 1.0 R \Rightarrow R = 8.0 \Omega$

Substituting the value of $R$ into the first equation:

$14.4 = 1.75 \times 8.0 + e$

$14.4 = 14.0 + e$

$e = 0.4 \text{ V}$

questions.q: An arrangement designed to measure the emf $\mathcal{E}$ and internal resistance $r$ of a battery is depicted in the figure. The voltmeter possesses a very high resistance, whereas the ammeter has some resistance. While the switch $S$ is open, the voltmeter indicates $1.52\text{ V}$. Once the switch is closed, the voltmeter's reading decreases to $1.45\text{ V}$ and the ammeter displays $1.0\text{ A}$. Calculate the emf and the internal resistance of the battery.
questions.solution:
When the switch $S$ is open, the current in the circuit is zero. The voltmeter measures the emf of the battery.

$\mathcal{E} = 1.52\text{ V}$

When the switch $S$ is closed, a current $I = 1.0\text{ A}$ flows through the circuit. The voltmeter measures the terminal voltage $V$ across the battery.

The terminal voltage is given by:

$V = \mathcal{E} - Ir$

Substituting the given values:

$1.45 = 1.52 - (1.0)r$

$r = 1.52 - 1.45 = 0.07\text{ }\Omega$

The emf is $1.52\text{ V}$ and the internal resistance is $0.07\text{ }\Omega$.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: When connected across an external resistor, the potential difference between the terminals of a battery having an emf of $6.0 \text{ V}$ and an internal resistance of $1 \Omega$ drops to $5.8 \text{ V}$. Determine the resistance of the external resistor.
questions.solution:
Given $E = 6.0 \text{ V}$, $r = 1 \Omega$, and $V = 5.8 \text{ V}$.

The terminal potential difference of the battery is given by $V = E - Ir$.

Substituting the given values:

$5.8 = 6.0 - I(1)$

$I = 0.2 \text{ A}$

Using Ohm's law for the external resistor, $V = IR$.

$5.8 = 0.2 \times R$

$R = \dfrac{5.8}{0.2} = 29 \Omega$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: When a $6.0 \text{ V}$ battery is being charged by a current of $2.0 \text{ A}$, the potential difference across its terminals is $7.2 \text{ V}$. Determine the internal resistance of the battery.
questions.solution:
During the charging of a battery, the terminal potential difference $V$ is given by the equation:

$V = E + Ir$

where $E$ is the emf of the battery, $I$ is the charging current, and $r$ is the internal resistance.

Given values are:
$V = 7.2 \text{ V}$
$E = 6.0 \text{ V}$
$I = 2.0 \text{ A}$

Substituting the given values into the equation:

$7.2 = 6.0 + 2.0r$

$2.0r = 1.2$

$r = \dfrac{1.2}{2.0} = 0.6 \ \Omega$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: When fully discharged, an accumulator battery of emf $6 \text{ V}$ possesses an internal resistance of $10 \Omega$. During the charging process, its internal resistance drops to $1 \Omega$. The battery, starting from its completely discharged state, is connected to a charger that provides a constant potential difference of $9 \text{ V}$. Calculate the current passing through the battery immediately after the circuit is connected.
questions.solution:
The current $I$ passing through a battery during the charging process is given by the relation $V = E + Ir$, where $V$ is the potential difference provided by the charger, $E$ is the emf of the battery, and $r$ is its internal resistance.

Immediately after the circuit is connected, the battery is still in its completely discharged state. Therefore, the internal resistance of the battery is $r = 10 \Omega$.

Substituting the given values $V = 9 \text{ V}$, $E = 6 \text{ V}$, and $r = 10 \Omega$ into the formula:

$I = \dfrac{V - E}{r}$

$I = \dfrac{9 - 6}{10}$

$I = \dfrac{3}{10} = 0.3 \text{ A}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: When fully discharged, an accumulator battery of emf $6 \text{ V}$ possesses an internal resistance of $10 \Omega$. During the charging process, its internal resistance drops to $1 \Omega$. The battery, starting from its completely discharged state, is connected to a charger that provides a constant potential difference of $9 \text{ V}$. Calculate the current passing through the battery after a long period once it is completely charged.
questions.solution:
The emf of the battery is $E = 6 \text{ V}$.

The constant potential difference provided by the charger is $V = 9 \text{ V}$.

When the battery is completely charged, its internal resistance drops to $r = 1 \Omega$.

During the charging process, the current $I$ flows into the positive terminal of the battery. The net potential difference driving the current is $V - E$.

Using Ohm's law, the current passing through the battery is given by:

$I = \dfrac{V - E}{r}$

Substituting the given values:

$I = \dfrac{9 - 6}{1} = 3 \text{ A}$

questions.q: Calculate the value of the ratio $i_1/i_2$ for the circuits shown in the figure, provided that the external resistance is $R = 10 \text{ }\Omega$.
questions.solution:
For the first circuit, the two cells are connected in series and aid each other.

The equivalent EMF is $E_1 = 6 + 6 = 12 \text{ V}$.

The equivalent internal resistance is $r_1 = 1 + 1 = 2 \text{ } \Omega$.

The current $i_1$ in the circuit is given by:

$i_1 = \dfrac{E_1}{R + r_1} = \dfrac{12}{10 + 2} = 1 \text{ A}$

For the second circuit, the two cells are connected in parallel.

The equivalent EMF is $E_2 = \dfrac{\dfrac{6}{1} + \dfrac{6}{1}}{\dfrac{1}{1} + \dfrac{1}{1}} = 6 \text{ V}$.

The equivalent internal resistance is $r_2 = \dfrac{1 \times 1}{1 + 1} = 0.5 \text{ } \Omega$.

The current $i_2$ in the circuit is given by:

$i_2 = \dfrac{E_2}{R + r_2} = \dfrac{6}{10 + 0.5} = \dfrac{6}{10.5} = \dfrac{4}{7} \text{ A}$

The ratio of the currents is:

$\dfrac{i_1}{i_2} = \dfrac{1}{\dfrac{4}{7}} = \dfrac{7}{4} = 1.75$

The total current $I$ flowing through the external resistance $R$ is given by $I = \dfrac{\mathcal{E}_{eq}}{R + r_{eq}}$.

Substituting the values, we get $I = \dfrac{n_1 \mathcal{E}}{R + \dfrac{n_1 r}{n_2}}$.

questions.q: Consider $N = n_1 n_2$ identical cells, each having an emf $\mathcal{E}$ and an internal resistance $r$. Assume $n_1$ cells are connected in series to form a line, and $n_2$ such lines are connected in parallel. This combination supplies current to an external resistance $R$. Assuming $n_1$ and $n_2$ can be varied continuously, determine the relation between $n_1$, $n_2$, $R$, and $r$ that yields the maximum current in $R$.
questions.solution:
Equivalent emf of one row of $n_1$ cells in series is $n_1 \mathcal{E}$ and its internal resistance is $n_1 r$.

Since $n_2$ such rows are connected in parallel, the equivalent emf of the entire combination remains $E_{eq} = n_1 \mathcal{E}$ and the equivalent internal resistance is $r_{eq} = \dfrac{n_1 r}{n_2}$.

The current $I$ through the external resistance $R$ is given by:

$I = \dfrac{E_{eq}}{R + r_{eq}} = \dfrac{n_1 \mathcal{E}}{R + \dfrac{n_1 r}{n_2}} = \dfrac{n_1 n_2 \mathcal{E}}{n_2 R + n_1 r}$

Since the total number of cells $N = n_1 n_2$ is constant, the numerator $N \mathcal{E}$ is constant. To maximize the current $I$, the denominator $n_2 R + n_1 r$ must be minimized.

We can rewrite the denominator as:

$n_2 R + n_1 r = \left( \sqrt{n_2 R} - \sqrt{n_1 r} \right)^2 + 2 \sqrt{n_1 n_2 R r}$

For the denominator to be minimum, the squared term must be zero:

$\sqrt{n_2 R} - \sqrt{n_1 r} = 0$

$n_2 R = n_1 r$

This gives the condition $r n_1 = R n_2$.

questions.q: A battery with an emf of $100 \text{ V}$ and a resistor having a resistance of $10 \text{ k}\Omega$ are connected in series. This arrangement serves as a source to deliver current to an external resistance $R$. Provided that $R$ does not exceed $100 \Omega$, the current flowing through it remains constant up to two significant digits. Determine the value of this current. (This illustrates the fundamental principle of a constant-current source.)
questions.solution:
The total resistance of the circuit is $R_{eq} = 10 \text{ k}\Omega + R = 10000 + R$.

Since $R \le 100 \Omega$, we have $R \ll 10000 \Omega$.

Therefore, the equivalent resistance is approximately $R_{eq} \approx 10000 \Omega$.

The current flowing through the external resistance is given by Ohm's law:

$I = \dfrac{E}{R_{eq}} \approx \dfrac{100}{10000} = 0.01 \text{ A}$

This current remains approximately constant for small values of $R$, acting as a constant-current source.

questions.q: In the circuit shown in the figure, the rheostat has a resistance of $30\text{ }\Omega$. Assuming the resistance of the ammeter is negligible, calculate the minimum and maximum currents passing through the ammeter as the rheostat is varied.
questions.solution:
The equivalent resistance of the parallel combination of $10\text{ }\Omega$ and $20\text{ }\Omega$ resistors is:

$R_p = \dfrac{10 \times 20}{10 + 20} = \dfrac{200}{30} = \dfrac{20}{3}\text{ }\Omega$

The total resistance of the circuit is the sum of $R_p$ and the resistance of the rheostat $R_v$ included in the circuit:

$R_{eq} = R_p + R_v = \dfrac{20}{3} + R_v$

The current in the circuit is given by Ohm's law:

$I = \dfrac{V}{R_{eq}} = \dfrac{5.5}{\dfrac{20}{3} + R_v}$

For maximum current, the rheostat resistance should be minimum, i.e., $R_v = 0\text{ }\Omega$:

$I_{max} = \dfrac{5.5}{\dfrac{20}{3} + 0} = \dfrac{5.5 \times 3}{20} = \dfrac{16.5}{20} = 0.825\text{ A} \approx 0.83\text{ A}$

For minimum current, the rheostat resistance should be maximum, i.e., $R_v = 30\text{ }\Omega$:

$I_{min} = \dfrac{5.5}{\dfrac{20}{3} + 30} = \dfrac{5.5}{\dfrac{110}{3}} = \dfrac{5.5 \times 3}{110} = \dfrac{16.5}{110} = 0.15\text{ A}$

Thus, the minimum and maximum currents are $0.15\text{ A}$ and $0.83\text{ A}$ respectively.

Given the resistance of each bulb, $R = 180 \Omega$.

According to Ohm's law, the total current $I$ delivered by the battery is:

$I = \dfrac{V}{R_{eq}} = \dfrac{60}{60} = 1.0 \text{ A}$

questions.solution:
To obtain the maximum resistance, all the resistors must be connected in series.

$R_\max = R_1 + R_2 + R_3$

$R_\max = 20 + 50 + 100 = 170 \Omega$

To obtain the minimum resistance, all the resistors must be connected in parallel.

$\dfrac{1}{R_\min} = \dfrac{1}{R_1} + \dfrac{1}{R_2} + \dfrac{1}{R_3}$

$\dfrac{1}{R_\min} = \dfrac{1}{20} + \dfrac{1}{50} + \dfrac{1}{100}$

$\dfrac{1}{R_\min} = \dfrac{5 + 2 + 1}{100} = \dfrac{8}{100}$

$R_\min = \dfrac{100}{8} = 12.5 \Omega$

The minimum and maximum resistances are $12.5 \Omega$ and $170 \Omega$ respectively.

questions.q: A bulb is constructed using two filaments. A switch allows the filaments to be used either individually or in parallel. When connected to a $15 \text{ V}$ battery, the bulb can operate at $5 \text{ W}$, $10 \text{ W}$, or $15 \text{ W}$. Determine the resistances of the filaments.
questions.solution:
The power dissipated by a resistance $R$ across a constant voltage $V$ is given by $P = \dfrac{V^2}{R}$.

When two filaments are connected in parallel, the total power is the sum of their individual powers, $P_p = P_1 + P_2$.

Given the possible power outputs are $5 \text{ W}$, $10 \text{ W}$, and $15 \text{ W}$. Since $5 + 10 = 15$, the individual powers of the filaments must be $P_1 = 5 \text{ W}$ and $P_2 = 10 \text{ W}$. The $15 \text{ W}$ output corresponds to the filaments connected in parallel.

For the first filament, the resistance is:

$R_1 = \dfrac{V^2}{P_1} = \dfrac{15^2}{5} = \dfrac{225}{5} = 45 \Omega$

For the second filament, the resistance is:

$R_2 = \dfrac{V^2}{P_2} = \dfrac{15^2}{10} = \dfrac{225}{10} = 22.5 \Omega$

The resistances of the filaments are $45 \Omega$ and $22.5 \Omega$.

questions.solution:
Let the voltage of the ideal battery be $V$ and the resistance of the first resistor be $R$.

Initially, the current is $5 \text{ A}$, so:

$I_1 = \dfrac{V}{R} = 5 \Rightarrow V = 5R$

When a $10 \Omega$ resistor is connected in parallel, the equivalent resistance becomes:

$R_{eq} = \dfrac{10R}{10 + R}$

The new current is $6 \text{ A}$, so:

$I_2 = \dfrac{V}{R_{eq}} = 6$

Substituting $V = 5R$ and $R_{eq}$ into the equation:

$\dfrac{5R}{\dfrac{10R}{10 + R}} = 6$

$\dfrac{5(10 + R)}{10} = 6$

$\dfrac{10 + R}{2} = 6$

$10 + R = 12$

$R = 2 \Omega$

Total resistance of the wire is $15.0 \Omega$.

Since the wire is bent into a regular hexagon, it has $6$ equal sides. The resistance of each side is $R = \dfrac{15.0}{6} = 2.5 \Omega$.

The points $A$ and $B$ are adjacent vertices. The equivalent circuit consists of two parallel paths between $A$ and $B$:
1. The direct path along the side $AB$ with resistance $R_{1} = R = 2.5 \Omega$.
2. The path through the remaining five sides with resistance $R_{2} = 5R = 12.5 \Omega$.

The equivalent resistance $R_{eq}$ is given by the parallel combination of $R_{1}$ and $R_{2}$:

$R_{eq} = \dfrac{R_{1} R_{2}}{R_{1} + R_{2}} = \dfrac{2.5 \times 12.5}{2.5 + 12.5}$

Total resistance of the wire, $R = 15.0 \Omega$

questions.q: A portion of an electric circuit is depicted in the figure. The electric potentials at points $a$, $b$, and $c$ are given as $30 \text{ V}$, $12 \text{ V}$, and $2 \text{ V}$, respectively. Determine the currents flowing through each of the three resistors.
options: $1 \text{ A}$ through $10 \text{ }\Omega$, $0.6 \text{ A}$ through $20 \text{ }\Omega$, and $0.4 \text{ A}$ through $30 \text{ }\Omega$
$2 \text{ A}$ through $10 \text{ }\Omega$, $0.8 \text{ A}$ through $20 \text{ }\Omega$, and $1.2 \text{ A}$ through $30 \text{ }\Omega$

questions.solution:
Let the electric potential at the junction of the three resistors be $V$.

Applying Kirchhoff's Current Law (KCL) at the junction, the sum of currents leaving the junction is zero. Assuming current flows from $a$ to the junction, and from the junction to $b$ and $c$:

$\dfrac{V_a - V}{10} = \dfrac{V - V_b}{20} + \dfrac{V - V_c}{30}$

Given that $V_a = 30 \text{ V}$, $V_b = 12 \text{ V}$, and $V_c = 2 \text{ V}$, we substitute these values into the equation:

$\dfrac{30 - V}{10} = \dfrac{V - 12}{20} + \dfrac{V - 2}{30}$

Multiplying the entire equation by $60$ to clear the denominators:

$6(30 - V) = 3(V - 12) + 2(V - 2)$

$180 - 6V = 3V - 36 + 2V - 4$

$180 - 6V = 5V - 40$

$11V = 220 \implies V = 20 \text{ V}$

Now, we calculate the current through each resistor:

Current through the $10 \text{ }\Omega$ resistor:
$I_{10} = \dfrac{V_a - V}{10} = \dfrac{30 - 20}{10} = 1 \text{ A}$

Current through the $20 \text{ }\Omega$ resistor:
$I_{20} = \dfrac{V - V_b}{20} = \dfrac{20 - 12}{20} = \dfrac{8}{20} = 0.4 \text{ A}$

Current through the $30 \text{ }\Omega$ resistor:
$I_{30} = \dfrac{V - V_c}{30} = \dfrac{20 - 2}{30} = \dfrac{18}{30} = 0.6 \text{ A}$

$V_{net} = 10\text{ V} - 10\text{ V} = 0\text{ V}$
Since resistor $b$ is connected across these two points, the potential difference across it is $0\text{ V}$.
The current through resistor $b$ is:
$I_b = \dfrac{0\text{ V}}{10\text{ }\Omega} = 0\text{ A}$

questions.q: Determine the potential difference $V_a - V_b$ for the electrical circuits presented in the figure.
questions.solution:
Let the potential at node b be $V_b = 0$. The potential difference to be found is $V_a - V_b = V_a$.

Both circuits (a) and (b) consist of three parallel branches connected between nodes a and b. The first branch contains a battery $\mathcal{E}_1$ and a resistor $R_1$, with the positive terminal of $\mathcal{E}_1$ connected to node a. The second branch contains only a resistor $R_3$. The third branch contains a battery $\mathcal{E}_2$ and a resistor $R_2$, with the positive terminal of $\mathcal{E}_2$ connected to node a.

Applying Kirchhoff's Current Law at node a, the sum of currents leaving the node must be zero:

$\dfrac{V_a - \mathcal{E}_1}{R_1} + \dfrac{V_a - 0}{R_3} + \dfrac{V_a - \mathcal{E}_2}{R_2} = 0$

Grouping the terms with $V_a$ on one side:

$V_a \left( \dfrac{1}{R_1} + \dfrac{1}{R_2} + \dfrac{1}{R_3} \right) - \dfrac{\mathcal{E}_1}{R_1} - \dfrac{\mathcal{E}_2}{R_2} = 0$

$V_a \left( \dfrac{1}{R_1} + \dfrac{1}{R_2} + \dfrac{1}{R_3} \right) = \dfrac{\mathcal{E}_1}{R_1} + \dfrac{\mathcal{E}_2}{R_2}$

$V_a = \dfrac{\dfrac{\mathcal{E}_1}{R_1} + \dfrac{\mathcal{E}_2}{R_2}}{\dfrac{1}{R_1} + \dfrac{1}{R_2} + \dfrac{1}{R_3}}$

This result can also be directly written using Millman's theorem.

Answer: $\dfrac{\dfrac{\mathcal{E}_1}{R_1} + \dfrac{\mathcal{E}_2}{R_2}}{\dfrac{1}{R_1} + \dfrac{1}{R_2} + \dfrac{1}{R_3}}$

questions.solution:
Using Millman's theorem, the equivalent EMF of the parallel combination of the three branches gives the potential difference between nodes A and B. Taking the potential at B to be higher than A (due to the orientation of the batteries):

$V_B - V_A = \dfrac{\dfrac{\mathcal{E}_1}{r_1} + \dfrac{\mathcal{E}_2}{r_2} + \dfrac{\mathcal{E}_3}{r_3}}{\dfrac{1}{r_1} + \dfrac{1}{r_2} + \dfrac{1}{r_3}}$

Substituting the given values:

The potential difference between A and B is $2 \text{ V}$.

Let the currents flowing from A to B in the three branches be $i_1$, $i_2$, and $i_3$ respectively. Applying Kirchhoff's Voltage Law for each branch from A to B:

$V_A - i_1 r_1 + \mathcal{E}_1 = V_B \Rightarrow i_1 = \dfrac{\mathcal{E}_1 - (V_B - V_A)}{r_1}$

$i_1 = \dfrac{3 - 2}{1} = 1 \text{ A}$

questions.q: Determine the equivalent resistance between the points $a$ and $b$ for the circuits displayed in the figure. Every resistor has a resistance $r$.
questions.solution:
For the first circuit, let the vertices of the triangle be $a$, $b$, and $c$ (top), and the central node be $o$. The circuit is symmetric about the vertical axis passing through $c$ and $o$. When a potential difference is applied across $a$ and $b$, the nodes $c$ and $o$ will be at the same potential. Since $V_c = V_o$, no current flows through the resistor connecting $c$ and $o$, so it can be removed from the circuit. The simplified circuit consists of three parallel branches between $a$ and $b$. The first branch is the direct resistor between $a$ and $b$ with resistance $r$. The second branch is the series combination of resistors $ac$ and $cb$, with resistance $r + r = 2r$. The third branch is the series combination of resistors $ao$ and $ob$, with resistance $r + r = 2r$. The equivalent resistance $R_a$ is given by $\dfrac{1}{R_a} = \dfrac{1}{r} + \dfrac{1}{2r} + \dfrac{1}{2r} = \dfrac{2}{r}$, which gives $R_a = \dfrac{r}{2}$.

For the second circuit, the structure is a hexagon with a central node $o$. Let the nodes on the perimeter be $a, c, d, b, f, e$ in clockwise order. The circuit is symmetric about the vertical axis passing through $o$ and the midpoints of resistors $cd$ and $ef$. If a voltage $2V$ is applied between $a$ and $b$ such that $V_a = V$ and $V_b = -V$, the potential along the vertical axis of symmetry is zero. The circuit can be split into two identical halves (left and right) in series. The left half consists of nodes $a, c, e$ and the grounded points (node $o$ and the midpoints of $cd$ and $ef$). Node $c$ is connected to ground via resistor $co$ (resistance $r$) and the left half of resistor $cd$ (resistance $r/2$). These two are in parallel, so the equivalent resistance from $c$ to ground is $R_{c,gnd} = \dfrac{r \times (r/2)}{r + r/2} = \dfrac{r}{3}$. Similarly, the equivalent resistance from node $e$ to ground is $R_{e,gnd} = \dfrac{r}{3}$. From node $a$, there are three parallel paths to ground. The first path is through $c$ to ground with resistance $R_{ac} + R_{c,gnd} = r + \dfrac{r}{3} = \dfrac{4r}{3}$. The second path is through $e$ to ground with resistance $R_{ae} + R_{e,gnd} = r + \dfrac{r}{3} = \dfrac{4r}{3}$. The third path is directly through $o$ to ground with resistance $R_{ao} = r$. The equivalent resistance of the left half, $R_{left}$, is given by $\dfrac{1}{R_{left}} = \dfrac{1}{4r/3} + \dfrac{1}{4r/3} + \dfrac{1}{r} = \dfrac{3}{4r} + \dfrac{3}{4r} + \dfrac{1}{r} = \dfrac{6}{4r} + \dfrac{1}{r} = \dfrac{3}{2r} + \dfrac{1}{r} = \dfrac{5}{2r}$. This gives $R_{left} = \dfrac{2r}{5}$. The total equivalent resistance between $a$ and $b$ is $R_b = 2 \times R_{left} = 2 \times \dfrac{2r}{5} = \dfrac{4r}{5}$.

Answer: (a) $\dfrac{r}{2}$, (b) $\dfrac{4r}{5}$

questions.q: Twelve wires, each with an equal resistance $r$, are connected to form a cube as shown in the figure. Calculate the equivalent resistance between the diagonally opposite points $a$ and $f$.
questions.solution:
Let the total current entering at junction $a$ be $I$ and leaving at junction $f$ be $I$.

Due to the symmetry of the cube, the current divides equally into three identical paths at junction $a$.

Current in branches $ab$, $ad$, and $ah$ is $\dfrac{I}{3}$.

At junction $b$, the current $\dfrac{I}{3}$ further divides equally into branches $bc$ and $be$ because the paths to $f$ are symmetric.

Current in branches $bc$ and $be$ is $\dfrac{I}{6}$.

Similarly, the current in branches $dc$, $dg$, $he$, and $hg$ is $\dfrac{I}{6}$.

At junction $c$, currents from $bc$ and $dc$ combine. So, the current in branch $cf$ is $\dfrac{I}{6} + \dfrac{I}{6} = \dfrac{I}{3}$.

The potential difference between points $a$ and $f$ along the path $a \rightarrow b \rightarrow c \rightarrow f$ is:

$V_{af} = V_{ab} + V_{bc} + V_{cf}$

$V_{af} = \left(\dfrac{I}{3}\right)r + \left(\dfrac{I}{6}\right)r + \left(\dfrac{I}{3}\right)r$

$V_{af} = Ir \left(\dfrac{1}{3} + \dfrac{1}{6} + \dfrac{1}{3}\right) = \dfrac{5}{6}Ir$

The equivalent resistance $R_{eq}$ is given by:

$R_{eq} = \dfrac{V_{af}}{I} = \dfrac{5}{6}r$

questions.q: Consider an infinite ladder constructed using $1\ \Omega$ and $2\ \Omega$ resistors, as shown in the figure. Determine the effective resistance between points $A$ and $B$.
questions.solution:
Let the effective resistance of the infinite ladder between points A and B be $R$.

Since the ladder is infinite, removing the first repeating unit (one $1\ \Omega$ resistor in series and one $2\ \Omega$ resistor in parallel) leaves an identical infinite ladder across the next nodes. Therefore, the resistance of the remaining infinite ladder is also $R$.

The equivalent circuit can be simplified to a $1\ \Omega$ resistor in series with the parallel combination of a $2\ \Omega$ resistor and $R$.

The equation for the equivalent resistance is:
$R = 1 + \dfrac{2R}{2 + R}$

Solving for $R$:
$R = \dfrac{2 + R + 2R}{2 + R}$

$R = \dfrac{3R + 2}{R + 2}$

$R(R + 2) = 3R + 2$

$R^2 + 2R = 3R + 2$

$R^2 - R - 2 = 0$

Factorizing the quadratic equation:
$(R - 2)(R + 1) = 0$

Since resistance cannot be negative, we discard $R = -1\ \Omega$.

Thus, $R = 2\ \Omega$.

questions.q: An infinite ladder is constructed with $1\ \Omega$ and $2\ \Omega$ resistors. It consists of repeating sections, each containing a $1\ \Omega$ resistor in the top branch and a $2\ \Omega$ resistor connecting the top and bottom branches. The bottom branch is a zero-resistance wire. A $6\text{ V}$ battery is connected across the input terminals. Calculate the current passing through the $2\ \Omega$ resistor located closest to the battery.
questions.solution:
Let the equivalent resistance of the infinite ladder across the input terminals be $R_{eq}$.

Since the ladder is infinite, removing the first repeating unit leaves the equivalent resistance unchanged. Thus, the circuit can be modeled as a $1\ \Omega$ resistor in series with a parallel combination of a $2\ \Omega$ resistor and $R_{eq}$.

The equivalent resistance is given by:

$R_{eq} = 1 + \dfrac{2 R_{eq}}{2 + R_{eq}}$

$R_{eq}(2 + R_{eq}) = 2 + R_{eq} + 2 R_{eq}$

$R_{eq}^2 + 2 R_{eq} = 2 + 3 R_{eq}$

$R_{eq}^2 - R_{eq} - 2 = 0$

$(R_{eq} - 2)(R_{eq} + 1) = 0$

Since resistance cannot be negative, $R_{eq} = 2\ \Omega$.

The total current drawn from the $6\text{ V}$ battery is:

$I = \dfrac{V}{R_{eq}} = \dfrac{6}{2} = 3\text{ A}$

This total current flows through the first $1\ \Omega$ resistor. At the first junction, the current splits into two parallel branches: the first $2\ \Omega$ resistor and the rest of the infinite ladder.

The resistance of the rest of the infinite ladder is also $R_{eq} = 2\ \Omega$. Since the two parallel branches have equal resistance ($2\ \Omega$ each), the current divides equally between them.

The current passing through the $2\ \Omega$ resistor closest to the battery is:

$I_{2\Omega} = \dfrac{I}{2} = \dfrac{3}{2} = 1.5\text{ A}$

questions.q: In the circuit depicted in the figure, the battery has an electromotive force $\mathcal{E}$ of $4.3 \text{ V}$ and an internal resistance $r$ of $1.0 \text{ }\Omega$. The external resistance $R$ is $50 \text{ }\Omega$. The resistances of the ammeter and the voltmeter are $2.0 \text{ }\Omega$ and $200 \text{ }\Omega$, respectively. Determine the readings of the ammeter and the voltmeter in the given switch configuration.
questions.solution:
Based on the given circuit diagram, the switch $S$ connects the voltmeter in parallel with the external resistance $R$ only.

First, we calculate the equivalent resistance of the parallel combination of the resistor $R$ and the voltmeter $R_V$:
$R_p = \dfrac{R \times R_V}{R + R_V}$
Substituting the given values ($R = 50 \text{ }\Omega$, $R_V = 200 \text{ }\Omega$):
$R_p = \dfrac{50 \times 200}{50 + 200} = \dfrac{10000}{250} = 40 \text{ }\Omega$

This parallel combination is in series with the ammeter ($R_A = 2.0 \text{ }\Omega$) and the internal resistance of the battery ($r = 1.0 \text{ }\Omega$). The total equivalent resistance of the circuit is:
$R_{eq} = R_p + R_A + r$
$R_{eq} = 40 + 2.0 + 1.0 = 43 \text{ }\Omega$

The total current $I$ flowing through the main circuit, which is also the reading of the ammeter, is given by Ohm's law:
$I = \dfrac{\mathcal{E}}{R_{eq}}$
$I = \dfrac{4.3}{43} = 0.1 \text{ A}$

The voltmeter measures the potential difference across the parallel combination $R_p$. This voltage $V$ is:
$V = I \times R_p$
$V = 0.1 \times 40 = 4.0 \text{ V}$

Therefore, the ammeter reads $0.1 \text{ A}$ and the voltmeter reads $4.0 \text{ V}$.

Answer: $0.1 \text{ A}$, $4.0 \text{ V}$

The external resistance $R$ is $50 \text{ }\Omega$. The resistances of the ammeter and voltmeter are $2.0 \text{ }\Omega$ and $200 \text{ }\Omega$ respectively. The switch is thrown to the other side such that the voltmeter is now connected across the series combination of $R$ and the ammeter. What will be the readings of the two meters now?
questions.solution:
When the switch is thrown to the other side, the voltmeter is connected in parallel with the series combination of the resistor $R$ and the ammeter.

Resistance of the series combination of $R$ and the ammeter:
$R_s = R + R_A = 50 + 2.0 = 52 \text{ }\Omega$

Equivalent resistance of the parallel combination of the voltmeter and $R_s$:
$R_p = \dfrac{R_s R_V}{R_s + R_V} = \dfrac{52 \times 200}{52 + 200} = \dfrac{10400}{252} = \dfrac{2600}{63} \text{ }\Omega$

Total equivalent resistance of the circuit including the internal resistance of the battery:
$R_{eq} = R_p + r = \dfrac{2600}{63} + 1.0 = \dfrac{2663}{63} \text{ }\Omega$

Total current drawn from the battery:
$I = \dfrac{\mathcal{E}}{R_{eq}} = \dfrac{4.3}{\dfrac{2663}{63}} = \dfrac{270.9}{2663} \text{ A}$

The voltmeter reading is the potential difference across the parallel combination:
$V = I \times R_p = \dfrac{270.9}{2663} \times \dfrac{2600}{63} = \dfrac{4.3 \times 2600}{2663} = \dfrac{11180}{2663} \approx 4.2 \text{ V}$

The ammeter reading is the current flowing through the series combination of $R$ and the ammeter:
$I_A = \dfrac{V}{R_s} = \dfrac{\dfrac{11180}{2663}}{52} = \dfrac{215}{2663} \approx 0.08 \text{ A}$

Answer: $0.08 \text{ A}$, $4.2 \text{ V}$

$S = \dfrac{I_g R_g}{I - I_g}$

In a balanced meter bridge, the Wheatstone bridge principle is applicable as the galvanometer shows zero deflection. The ratio of the resistances is equal to the ratio of the corresponding balancing lengths of the wire.

Given:
Total length of the wire $AB = 50 \text{ cm}$
Balancing length $AD = 30 \text{ cm}$
Length $DB = 50 - 30 = 20 \text{ cm}$
Left resistance $= 6\ \Omega$
Right resistance $= R$

Applying the balanced Wheatstone bridge condition:
$\dfrac{6}{R} = \dfrac{AD}{DB}$

$\dfrac{6}{R} = \dfrac{30}{20}$

$\dfrac{6}{R} = \dfrac{3}{2}$

$R = \dfrac{6 \times 2}{3} = 4\ \Omega$

questions.q:
A $6\text{-volt}$ battery with negligible internal resistance is connected across a uniform wire $AB$ of length $100 \text{ cm}$. As shown in the figure, the positive terminal of another battery having an emf of $4 \text{ V}$ and an internal resistance of $1 \text{ }\Omega$ is joined to point $A$. Assume the potential at $B$ is zero. Determine the following:
(i) The potentials at points $A$ and $C$.
(ii) The distance from $A$ to the point $D$ on the wire $AB$ where the potential equals the potential at $C$.
(iii) The current through a wire if points $C$ and $D$ are connected by it.
(iv) The answers to (i) and (ii) if the $4 \text{ V}$ battery is replaced by a $7.5 \text{ V}$ battery.
options: (i) $6 \text{ V}$, $2 \text{ V}$; (ii) $33.3 \text{ cm}$; (iii) $1 \text{ A}$; (iv) $6 \text{ V}$, $-1.5 \text{ V}$, $25 \text{ cm}$
(i) $4 \text{ V}$, $2 \text{ V}$; (ii) $50 \text{ cm}$; (iii) zero; (iv) $4 \text{ V}$, $-3.5 \text{ V}$, no such point exists
(i) $6 \text{ V}$, $2 \text{ V}$; (ii) $66.7 \text{ cm}$; (iii) zero; (iv) $6 \text{ V}$, $-1.5 \text{ V}$, no such point exists
(i) $6 \text{ V}$, $4 \text{ V}$; (ii) $33.3 \text{ cm}$; (iii) $2 \text{ A}$; (iv) $6 \text{ V}$, $1.5 \text{ V}$, $75 \text{ cm}$
questions.solution:
Given $V_B = 0 \text{ V}$. The $6 \text{ V}$ battery is connected across the wire $AB$ with its positive terminal at $A$.

$V_A - V_B = 6 \text{ V} \Rightarrow V_A = 6 \text{ V}$

In the lower branch, the $4 \text{ V}$ battery has its positive terminal at $A$. Since the circuit is open at $C$, no current flows through the $1 \text{ }\Omega$ resistor, meaning there is no voltage drop across it.

$V_A - V_C = 4 \text{ V} \Rightarrow V_C = 6 - 4 = 2 \text{ V}$

Let $D$ be at a distance $x$ from $A$. The potential gradient along the wire $AB$ of length $100 \text{ cm}$ is:

$\lambda = \dfrac{V_A - V_B}{L} = \dfrac{6}{100} = 0.06 \text{ V/cm}$

The potential at $D$ is given by:

$V_D = V_A - \lambda x = 6 - 0.06x$

We require $V_D = V_C = 2 \text{ V}$:

$6 - 0.06x = 2 \Rightarrow 0.06x = 4 \Rightarrow x = \dfrac{400}{6} = 66.7 \text{ cm}$

If points $C$ and $D$ are connected, the potential difference between them is zero ($V_C = V_D = 2 \text{ V}$). Therefore, the current through the connecting wire will be zero.

If the $4 \text{ V}$ battery is replaced by a $7.5 \text{ V}$ battery, the new potential at $C$ becomes:

$V_C = V_A - 7.5 = 6 - 7.5 = -1.5 \text{ V}$

The potential on the wire $AB$ ranges from $6 \text{ V}$ at $A$ to $0 \text{ V}$ at $B$. Since $-1.5 \text{ V}$ is outside this range, no such point exists on the wire.

questions.q: Examine the potentiometer circuit arranged as shown in the figure. The potentiometer wire has a length of $600 \text{ cm}$. Determine the distance from point $A$ where the jockey must touch the wire to achieve zero deflection in the galvanometer.
questions.solution:
The total resistance of the primary circuit is the sum of the internal resistance of the battery and the resistance of the potentiometer wire:

$R_{\text{eq}} = r + R = r + 15r = 16r$

The current flowing through the primary circuit is:

$I = \dfrac{\mathcal{E}}{R_{\text{eq}}} = \dfrac{\mathcal{E}}{16r}$

The potential difference across the entire potentiometer wire of length $L$ is:

$V = I \times R = \left(\dfrac{\mathcal{E}}{16r}\right) \times 15r = \dfrac{15\mathcal{E}}{16}$

The potential gradient (potential drop per unit length) along the potentiometer wire is:

$k = \dfrac{V}{L} = \dfrac{15\mathcal{E}}{16L}$

For zero deflection in the galvanometer, the potential difference across the balancing length $x$ must be equal to the emf of the cell in the secondary circuit. Since no current flows through the galvanometer, the internal resistance $r$ of the secondary cell does not contribute to any potential drop.

$k x = \dfrac{\mathcal{E}}{2}$

Substituting the value of $k$:

$\left(\dfrac{15\mathcal{E}}{16L}\right) x = \dfrac{\mathcal{E}}{2}$

$x = \dfrac{16L}{2 \times 15} = \dfrac{8L}{15}$

Given the total length of the potentiometer wire is $L = 600 \text{ cm}$:

$x = \dfrac{8 \times 600}{15} = 8 \times 40 = 320 \text{ cm}$

questions.q: Consider a potentiometer circuit where the primary loop contains a battery of emf $\mathcal{E}$ and internal resistance $r$ connected across a potentiometer wire of resistance $15r$ and length $600 \text{ cm}$. A secondary branch, containing a battery of emf $\mathcal{E}/2$, a resistor $r$, and a galvanometer, is connected between one end (point $A$) of the wire and a jockey. The positive terminals of both batteries are joined at point $A$. If the jockey touches the wire at a distance of $560 \text{ cm}$ from $A$, what will be the current in the galvanometer?
questions.solution:
Let the total length of the potentiometer wire be $L = 600 \text{ cm}$ and its total resistance be $R = 15r$.
The jockey divides the wire into two segments at a distance $l = 560 \text{ cm}$ from point A. Let the point where the jockey touches be J, and the other end of the wire be B.
The resistance of the segment AJ is:
$R_{AJ} = \dfrac{l}{L} \times R = \dfrac{560}{600} \times 15r = 14r$
The resistance of the remaining segment JB is:
$R_{JB} = 15r - 14r = r$

We can simplify the primary circuit using Thevenin's theorem across the points A and J. First, we find the open-circuit voltage ($V_{th}$) and Thevenin resistance ($R_{th}$) by removing the secondary branch.
The primary circuit is a single loop containing the battery $\mathcal{E}$, its internal resistance $r$, and the potentiometer wire of resistance $15r$.
The total resistance of this primary loop is $R_{primary} = r + 15r = 16r$.
The current in the primary loop is:
$I_0 = \dfrac{\mathcal{E}}{16r}$
The open-circuit potential difference across AJ is:
$V_{th} = V_A - V_J = I_0 \times R_{AJ} = \left(\dfrac{\mathcal{E}}{16r}\right) \times 14r = \dfrac{7\mathcal{E}}{8}$

To find the Thevenin resistance $R_{th}$ across A and J, we short-circuit the battery $\mathcal{E}$. The resistance $R_{th}$ is the parallel combination of $R_{AJ}$ and the rest of the primary loop ($R_{JB} + r$):
$R_{th} = \dfrac{R_{AJ} \times (R_{JB} + r)}{R_{AJ} + (R_{JB} + r)} = \dfrac{14r \times (r + r)}{14r + 2r} = \dfrac{28r^2}{16r} = \dfrac{7r}{4}$

Now, we connect the secondary branch across the Thevenin equivalent circuit. The secondary branch contains a battery of emf $\mathcal{E}/2$ and a resistor $r$. Since the positive terminals of both batteries are connected at A, the batteries oppose each other in the equivalent loop.
The net EMF in the loop is:
$\mathcal{E}_{net} = V_{th} - \dfrac{\mathcal{E}}{2} = \dfrac{7\mathcal{E}}{8} - \dfrac{\mathcal{E}}{2} = \dfrac{3\mathcal{E}}{8}$
The total resistance in the equivalent loop is:
$R_{total} = R_{th} + r = \dfrac{7r}{4} + r = \dfrac{11r}{4}$

The current $I$ through the galvanometer is:
$I = \dfrac{\mathcal{E}_{net}}{R_{total}} = \dfrac{\dfrac{3\mathcal{E}}{8}}{\dfrac{11r}{4}} = \dfrac{3\mathcal{E}}{8} \times \dfrac{4}{11r} = \dfrac{3\mathcal{E}}{22r}$

Answer: $\dfrac{3\mathcal{E}}{22 r}$

questions.q: Determine the charge on the capacitor depicted in the accompanying figure.
questions.solution:
In steady state, the capacitor acts as an open circuit. The current flows only through the series combination of the resistors.

The equivalent resistance of the circuit is:
$R_{eq} = 10 \Omega + 20 \Omega = 30 \Omega$

The current in the circuit is:
$I = \dfrac{V}{R_{eq}} = \dfrac{2}{30} = \dfrac{1}{15} \text{ A}$

$V_C = I \times 10 = \dfrac{1}{15} \times 10 = \dfrac{2}{3} \text{ V}$

The charge on the capacitor is:
$Q = C V_C = 6 \mu\text{F} \times \dfrac{2}{3} \text{ V} = 4 \mu\text{C}$

questions.q: Determine the current in the $20 \text{ }\Omega$ resistor for the circuit shown in the figure.
questions.solution:
Taking the potential at node B as $0\text{ V}$ and at node A as $V_A$.

Applying Kirchhoff's Current Law (KCL) at node A:

$\dfrac{V_A - 5}{10} + \dfrac{V_A - 0}{20} + \dfrac{V_A - 5}{10} = 0$

Multiplying the equation by $20$ to clear the denominators:

$2(V_A - 5) + V_A + 2(V_A - 5) = 0$

$2V_A - 10 + V_A + 2V_A - 10 = 0$

$5V_A = 20 \Rightarrow V_A = 4\text{ V}$

The current through the $20\text{ }\Omega$ resistor is:

$I = \dfrac{V_A - V_B}{20} = \dfrac{4 - 0}{20} = 0.2\text{ A}$

questions.q: For the circuit shown in the related figure, if a capacitor having a capacitance of $4 \text{ }\mu\text{F}$ is connected between the points $A$ and $B$, determine the electrostatic energy stored in it during steady state.
questions.solution:
Let the potential at point B be $V_B = 0\text{ V}$.

In steady state, the capacitor acts as an open circuit, so it does not draw any DC current. The current distribution in the resistor network remains unchanged.

Applying Kirchhoff's Current Law (KCL) at node A:

$\dfrac{V_A - 5}{10} + \dfrac{V_A - 5}{10} + \dfrac{V_A - 0}{20} = 0$

Multiplying the equation by $20$, we get:

$2(V_A - 5) + 2(V_A - 5) + V_A = 0$

$4V_A - 20 + V_A = 0$

$5V_A = 20 \Rightarrow V_A = 4\text{ V}$

The potential difference across the capacitor connected between A and B is $V = V_A - V_B = 4\text{ V}$.

The electrostatic energy stored in the capacitor is given by:

$U = \dfrac{1}{2}CV^2$

$U = \dfrac{1}{2} \times 4\text{ }\mu\text{F} \times (4\text{ V})^2$

$U = 2 \times 16\text{ }\mu\text{J} = 32\text{ }\mu\text{J}$

questions.q: Determine the charges on the four capacitors having capacitances $1 \text{ }\mu\text{F}$, $2 \text{ }\mu\text{F}$, $3 \text{ }\mu\text{F}$, and $4 \text{ }\mu\text{F}$ as shown in the figure.
questions.solution:
In steady state, capacitors act as open circuits, so no direct current flows through the branches containing only capacitors.

Let the potential of the negative terminal of the $6\text{ V}$ battery be $0\text{ V}$ and the positive terminal be $6\text{ V}$. The left vertical wire is at $6\text{ V}$ and the right vertical wire is at $0\text{ V}$.

For the branch with $1\text{ }\Omega$ and $2\text{ }\Omega$ resistors, they are in series. The current through this branch is:
$I_1 = \dfrac{6}{1 + 2} = 2\text{ A}$

The potential at the node between the $1\text{ }\Omega$ and $2\text{ }\Omega$ resistors is:
$V_1 = 6 - (2 \times 1) = 4\text{ V}$

This node is connected to the node between the $1\text{ }\mu\text{F}$ and $2\text{ }\mu\text{F}$ capacitors, so the potential between these capacitors is also $4\text{ V}$.

The potential difference across the $1\text{ }\mu\text{F}$ capacitor is $6 - 4 = 2\text{ V}$. Its charge is:
$q_1 = 1\text{ }\mu\text{F} \times 2\text{ V} = 2\text{ }\mu\text{C}$

The potential difference across the $2\text{ }\mu\text{F}$ capacitor is $4 - 0 = 4\text{ V}$. Its charge is:
$q_2 = 2\text{ }\mu\text{F} \times 4\text{ V} = 8\text{ }\mu\text{C}$

For the branch with two $3\text{ }\Omega$ resistors, they are in series. The current through this branch is:
$I_2 = \dfrac{6}{3 + 3} = 1\text{ A}$

The potential at the node between the two $3\text{ }\Omega$ resistors is:
$V_2 = 6 - (1 \times 3) = 3\text{ V}$

This node is connected to the node between the $3\text{ }\mu\text{F}$ and $4\text{ }\mu\text{F}$ capacitors, so the potential between these capacitors is also $3\text{ V}$.

The potential difference across the $3\text{ }\mu\text{F}$ capacitor is $6 - 3 = 3\text{ V}$. Its charge is:
$q_3 = 3\text{ }\mu\text{F} \times 3\text{ V} = 9\text{ }\mu\text{C}$

The potential difference across the $4\text{ }\mu\text{F}$ capacitor is $3 - 0 = 3\text{ V}$. Its charge is:
$q_4 = 4\text{ }\mu\text{F} \times 3\text{ V} = 12\text{ }\mu\text{C}$

The charges on the four capacitors are $2\text{ }\mu\text{C}$, $8\text{ }\mu\text{C}$, $9\text{ }\mu\text{C}$, and $12\text{ }\mu\text{C}$ respectively.

Answer: $2 \text{ }\mu\text{C}$, $8 \text{ }\mu\text{C}$, $9 \text{ }\mu\text{C}$, and $12 \text{ }\mu\text{C}$

$I_2 = \dfrac{6}{3 + 3} = 1\text{ A}$

The potential at the node between the two $3\text{ }\Omega$ resistors is:
$V_2 = 6 - (1 \times 3) = 3\text{ V}$

This node is connected to the node between the $3\text{ }\mu\text{F}$ and $4\text{ }\mu\text{F}$ capacitors, so the potential between these capacitors is also $3\text{ V}$.

The potential difference across the $3\text{ }\mu\text{F}$ capacitor is $6 - 3 = 3\text{ V}$. Its charge is:
$q_3 = 3\text{ }\mu\text{F} \times 3\text{ V} = 9\text{ }\mu\text{C}$

The potential difference across the $4\text{ }\mu\text{F}$ capacitor is $3 - 0 = 3\text{ V}$. Its charge is:
$q_4 = 4\text{ }\mu\text{F} \times 3\text{ V} = 12\text{ }\mu\text{C}$

The charges on the four capacitors are $2\text{ }\mu\text{C}$, $8\text{ }\mu\text{C}$, $9\text{ }\mu\text{C}$, and $12\text{ }\mu\text{C}$ respectively.

Answer: $2 \text{ }\mu\text{C}$, $8 \text{ }\mu\text{C}$, $9 \text{ }\mu\text{C}$, and $12 \text{ }\mu\text{C}$

questions.q: Determine the potential difference between points $A$ and $B$, and between points $B$ and $C$, for the circuit shown in the figure in steady state.
questions.solution:
In steady state, the capacitors are fully charged and act as open circuits. Therefore, no direct current flows through the circuit ($I = 0$).

Since the current is zero, there is no voltage drop across the $20\ \Omega$ and $10\ \Omega$ resistors. The potential difference across the capacitor network, between points A and C, is equal to the electromotive force of the battery:

$V_A - V_C = 100\text{ V}$

Let us analyze the connections of the capacitors in the network. The left vertical wire is entirely at potential $V_A$, and the right vertical wire is entirely at potential $V_C$.

The top $3\ \mu\text{F}$ capacitor is connected between node A and node B. The middle horizontal wire is connected to the left vertical wire (node A). The vertical $3\ \mu\text{F}$ capacitor connects this middle wire to node B. Thus, both $3\ \mu\text{F}$ capacitors are connected in parallel between nodes A and B. Their equivalent capacitance is:

$C_{AB} = 3\ \mu\text{F} + 3\ \mu\text{F} = 6\ \mu\text{F}$

Similarly, the top $1\ \mu\text{F}$ capacitor is connected between node B and node C. The middle horizontal wire is connected to the right vertical wire (node C). The vertical $1\ \mu\text{F}$ capacitor connects this middle wire to node B. Thus, both $1\ \mu\text{F}$ capacitors are connected in parallel between nodes B and C. Their equivalent capacitance is:

$C_{BC} = 1\ \mu\text{F} + 1\ \mu\text{F} = 2\ \mu\text{F}$

The middle $1\ \mu\text{F}$ capacitor is connected directly between node A and node C. It is in parallel with the series combination of $C_{AB}$ and $C_{BC}$, and does not affect the potential at node B.

The equivalent capacitors $C_{AB}$ and $C_{BC}$ are in series across the potential difference of $100\text{ V}$. In a series combination, the potential difference across a capacitor is inversely proportional to its capacitance.

The potential difference between A and B is:

$V_{AB} = V_{AC} \times \dfrac{C_{BC}}{C_{AB} + C_{BC}}$

$V_{AB} = 100 \times \dfrac{2}{6 + 2} = 100 \times \dfrac{2}{8} = 25\text{ V}$

The potential difference between B and C is:

$V_{BC} = V_{AC} \times \dfrac{C_{AB}}{C_{AB} + C_{BC}}$

$V_{BC} = 100 \times \dfrac{6}{6 + 2} = 100 \times \dfrac{6}{8} = 75\text{ V}$

Answer: $25 \text{ V}$ and $75 \text{ V}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: At $t = 0$, a capacitance $C$, a resistance $R$, and an emf $\mathcal{E}$ are connected in series. Determine the maximum value of the potential difference across the resistor.
questions.solution:
At $t = 0$, the capacitor is uncharged, so the potential difference across it is zero, i.e., $V_C = 0$.

According to Kirchhoff's voltage law for the series RC circuit, $\mathcal{E} = V_R + V_C$.

Substituting $V_C = 0$ at $t = 0$, we get $V_R = \mathcal{E}$.

As time progresses, the capacitor charges up, increasing $V_C$ and decreasing $V_R$ since $V_R = \mathcal{E} e^{-t/RC}$.

Thus, the maximum potential difference across the resistor occurs at $t = 0$ and is equal to $\mathcal{E}$.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: At $t = 0$, a capacitance $C$, a resistance $R$, and an emf $\mathcal{E}$ are connected in series. Determine the maximum value of the current in the circuit.
questions.solution:
At $t = 0$, the capacitor is uncharged and acts as a short circuit.

The equation for the current in an RC series circuit during charging is given by $I = \dfrac{\mathcal{E}}{R} e^{-t / RC}$.

The maximum value of the current occurs at $t = 0$.

Substituting $t = 0$, we get $I_\max = \dfrac{\mathcal{E}}{R}$.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: At $t = 0$, a capacitance $C$, a resistance $R$, and an emf $\mathcal{E}$ are connected in series. Determine the maximum value of the potential difference across the capacitor.
questions.solution:
The charge on the capacitor in a series RC circuit as a function of time is given by:

$q(t) = C\mathcal{E}(1 - e^{-t/RC})$

The potential difference across the capacitor at any time $t$ is:

$V_C(t) = \dfrac{q(t)}{C} = \mathcal{E}(1 - e^{-t/RC})$

The maximum potential difference is attained at steady state, which corresponds to $t \rightarrow \infty$.

At $t \rightarrow \infty$, $e^{-t/RC} \rightarrow 0$.

Therefore, the maximum potential difference across the capacitor is:

$(V_C)_{\text\max} = \mathcal{E}(1 - 0) = \mathcal{E}$

Alternatively, at steady state, the capacitor acts as an open circuit. The current in the circuit becomes zero, so the potential drop across the resistor is zero. By Kirchhoff's voltage law, the entire emf $\mathcal{E}$ appears across the capacitor.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: At $t = 0$, a capacitance $C$, a resistance $R$, and an emf $\mathcal{E}$ are connected in series. Determine the maximum value of the energy stored in the capacitor.
questions.solution:
The charge on the capacitor at any time $t$ during the charging of an RC circuit is given by:

$q(t) = C \mathcal{E} (1 - e^{-t/RC})$

The energy stored in the capacitor at any time $t$ is:

$U(t) = \dfrac{q(t)^2}{2C}$

The maximum charge on the capacitor is reached in the steady state as $t \rightarrow \infty$:

$q_\max = C \mathcal{E}$

Substituting the maximum charge into the energy formula, the maximum energy stored in the capacitor is:

$U_\max = \dfrac{q_\max^2}{2C} = \dfrac{(C \mathcal{E})^2}{2C} = \dfrac{1}{2} C \mathcal{E}^2$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: At $t = 0$, a capacitance $C$, a resistance $R$, and an emf $\mathcal{E}$ are connected in series. Determine the maximum value of the power delivered by the battery.
questions.solution:
The current in a series RC circuit as a function of time is given by:

$I(t) = \dfrac{\mathcal{E}}{R} e^{-t/RC}$

The power delivered by the battery is the product of its emf and the current flowing through the circuit:

$P(t) = \mathcal{E} I(t) = \dfrac{\mathcal{E}^2}{R} e^{-t/RC}$

Since the exponential term $e^{-t/RC}$ is a decreasing function of time for $t \ge 0$, the power delivered by the battery is maximum at the initial moment, $t = 0$.

Substituting $t = 0$ into the power equation:

$P_\max = \dfrac{\mathcal{E}^2}{R} e^{0} = \dfrac{\mathcal{E}^2}{R}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: At $t = 0$, a capacitance $C$, a resistance $R$, and an emf $\mathcal{E}$ are connected in series. Determine the maximum value of the power converted into heat.
questions.solution:
The current in an RC series circuit during charging is given by $I = \dfrac{\mathcal{E}}{R} e^{-t/RC}$.

The power converted into heat is the power dissipated across the resistor, which is given by $P = I^2 R$.

Substituting the expression for current, we get:

$P = \left( \dfrac{\mathcal{E}}{R} e^{-t/RC} \right)^2 R = \dfrac{\mathcal{E}^2}{R} e^{-2t/RC}$

The power is maximum when the exponential term $e^{-2t/RC}$ is maximum. For $t \ge 0$, the maximum value occurs at $t = 0$, where $e^{-2t/RC} = 1$.

Therefore, the maximum power converted into heat is:

$P_{\max} = \dfrac{\mathcal{E}^2}{R}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A parallel-plate capacitor having a plate area of $20 \text{ cm}^2$ and a plate separation of $1.0 \text{ mm}$ is connected to a battery. The circuit has a resistance of $10 \text{ k}\Omega$. Determine the time constant of the circuit.
questions.solution:
The capacitance of a parallel-plate capacitor is given by $C = \dfrac{\varepsilon_0 A}{d}$

Substituting the given values:

$C = \dfrac{8.85 \times 10^{-12} \times 20 \times 10^{-4}}{1.0 \times 10^{-3}}$

$C = 17.7 \times 10^{-12} \text{ F}$

The time constant of the RC circuit is given by $\tau = RC$

$\tau = 10 \times 10^3 \times 17.7 \times 10^{-12}$

$\tau = 17.7 \times 10^{-8} \text{ s} = 0.177 \mu\text{s} \approx 0.18 \mu\text{s}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A $10 \mu\text{F}$ capacitor is connected to a battery with an emf of $2 \text{ V}$. It takes $50 \text{ ms}$ for the charge on the capacitor to reach $12.6 \mu\text{C}$. Determine the resistance of the circuit.
questions.solution:
Given $C = 10 \mu\text{F}$, $V = 2 \text{ V}$, $t = 50 \text{ ms}$, and $q = 12.6 \mu\text{C}$.

The maximum charge on the capacitor is $q_0 = CV = 10 \times 10^{-6} \times 2 = 20 \mu\text{C}$.

The charge on a capacitor during charging is given by $q = q_0(1 - e^{-t/RC})$.

Substituting the values:

$12.6 = 20(1 - e^{-t/RC})$

$1 - e^{-t/RC} = \dfrac{12.6}{20} = 0.63$

$e^{-t/RC} = 0.37$

Since $e^{-1} \approx 0.37$, we have $\dfrac{t}{RC} = 1$.

Therefore, $RC = t = 50 \text{ ms}$.

$R = \dfrac{50 \times 10^{-3}}{10 \times 10^{-6}} = 5 \times 10^3 \Omega = 5 \text{ k}\Omega$.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: Through a resistance of $100 \Omega$, a $20 \mu\text{F}$ capacitor is connected to a battery with an emf of $6.0 \text{ V}$. Determine the charge on the capacitor $2.0 \text{ ms}$ after making the connections.
questions.solution:
The maximum charge on the capacitor is given by $q_{0} = CV$.

$q_{0} = 20 \times 10^{-6} \times 6.0 = 120 \mu\text{C}$

The time constant of the $RC$ circuit is $\tau = RC$.

$\tau = 100 \times 20 \times 10^{-6} = 2.0 \times 10^{-3} \text{ s} = 2.0 \text{ ms}$

The charge on the capacitor at any time $t$ during charging is given by $q(t) = q_{0}(1 - e^{-t/\tau})$.

Substituting $t = 2.0 \text{ ms}$ and $\tau = 2.0 \text{ ms}$:

$q = 120(1 - e^{-2.0/2.0}) = 120(1 - e^{-1})$

Using $e \approx 2.718$, we have $e^{-1} \approx 0.368$.

$q = 120(1 - 0.368) = 120 \times 0.632 = 75.84 \mu\text{C}$

Rounding to the nearest integer, the charge is approximately $76 \mu\text{C}$.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: At $t = 0$, the plates of a capacitor of capacitance $10 ext{ }\mu\text{F}$, charged to $60 ext{ }\mu\text{C}$, are connected together by a wire having a resistance of $10 ext{ }\Omega$. Determine the charge on the capacitor in the circuit at $t = 0$.
questions.solution:
The charge on a discharging capacitor at any time $t$ is given by the equation $q(t) = q_0 e^{-t/RC}$.

Given the initial charge on the capacitor is $q_0 = 60 \mu\text{C}$.

Substituting $t = 0$ in the equation, we get:

$q(0) = 60 \times e^0 = 60 \mu\text{C}$

Thus, the charge on the capacitor at the instant the connection is made ($t = 0$) remains equal to its initial charge, which is $60 \mu\text{C}$.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: At $t = 0$, the plates of a capacitor of capacitance $10 ext{ }\mu\text{F}$, charged to $60 ext{ }\mu\text{C}$, are connected together by a wire having a resistance of $10 ext{ }\Omega$. Determine the charge on the capacitor in the circuit at $t = 30 ext{ }\mu\text{s}$.
questions.solution:
The time constant of the discharging RC circuit is given by $\tau = RC$.

Substituting the given values:
$\tau = 10 \times 10 \times 10^{-6} \text{ s} = 100 \mu\text{s}$

The charge on the capacitor during discharging is given by:
$q = q_0 e^{-t/\tau}$

Substituting $q_0 = 60 \mu\text{C}$ and $t = 30 \mu\text{s}$:
$q = 60 e^{-30/100} = 60 e^{-0.3} \mu\text{C}$

Using the approximation $e^{-0.3} \approx 0.74$:
$q \approx 60 \times 0.74 \mu\text{C} = 44.4 \mu\text{C}$

The closest value among the given options is $44 \mu\text{C}$.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: At $t = 0$, the plates of a capacitor of capacitance $10 ext{ }\mu\text{F}$, charged to $60 ext{ }\mu\text{C}$, are connected together by a wire having a resistance of $10 ext{ }\Omega$. Determine the charge on the capacitor in the circuit at $t = 120 ext{ }\mu\text{s}$.
questions.solution:
The charge on a discharging capacitor at time $t$ is given by the equation:

$q(t) = q_0 e^{-t/\tau}$

where the time constant is $\tau = RC$.

Given values are:
Initial charge, $q_0 = 60 \mu\text{C}$
Resistance, $R = 10 \Omega$
Capacitance, $C = 10 \mu\text{F}$
Time, $t = 120 \mu\text{s}$

Calculating the time constant $\tau$:

$\tau = 10 \Omega \times 10 \mu\text{F} = 100 \mu\text{s}$

Substituting the values into the discharging equation:

$q(120 \mu\text{s}) = 60 e^{-120/100}$

$q = 60 e^{-1.2}$

Using the approximate value $e^{-1.2} \approx 0.301$:

$q \approx 60 \times 0.301 \approx 18.06 \mu\text{C}$

Rounding to the nearest integer, the charge on the capacitor is $18 \mu\text{C}$.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: At $t = 0$, the plates of a capacitor of capacitance $10 ext{ }\mu\text{F}$, charged to $60 ext{ }\mu\text{C}$, are connected together by a wire having a resistance of $10 ext{ }\Omega$. Determine the charge on the capacitor in the circuit at $t = 1.0 ext{ ms}$.
questions.solution:
The discharging of a capacitor is given by the equation:

$q(t) = q_0 e^{-t / \tau}$

where $\tau = RC$ is the time constant of the circuit.

Given values are $C = 10 \mu\text{F}$, $R = 10 \Omega$, $q_0 = 60 \mu\text{C}$, and $t = 1.0 \text{ ms} = 10^{-3} \text{ s}$.

Calculating the time constant $\tau$:

$\tau = RC = 10 \times 10 \times 10^{-6} = 10^{-4} \text{ s}$

Substituting the values into the discharging equation:

$q(t) = 60 \times e^{-10^{-3} / 10^{-4}} \mu\text{C}$

$q(t) = 60 \times e^{-10} \mu\text{C}$

Using the approximate value $e^{10} \approx 22026$:

$q(t) = \dfrac{60}{22026} \mu\text{C} \approx 0.00272 \mu\text{C}$

Rounding to the nearest given option, the charge is approximately $0.003 \mu\text{C}$.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A capacitor with a capacitance of $8.0 \mu\text{F}$ is wired to a battery of emf $6.0 \text{ V}$ via a resistance of $24 \Omega$. Determine the current in the circuit immediately after the connections are made.
questions.solution:
Immediately after the connections are made, at $t = 0$, the uncharged capacitor acts as a short circuit.

The initial current in the circuit is limited only by the resistance.

The initial current $I_0$ is given by:

$I_0 = \dfrac{V}{R}$

Substituting the given values:

$I_0 = \dfrac{6.0}{24} = 0.25 \text{ A}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A capacitor with a capacitance of $8.0 \mu\text{F}$ is wired to a battery of emf $6.0 \text{ V}$ via a resistance of $24 \Omega$. Determine the current in the circuit exactly one time constant after the connections are made.
questions.solution:
The current in an RC circuit during charging is given by the equation:

$I(t) = I_0 e^{-t/\tau}$

where $I_0 = \dfrac{V}{R}$ is the initial current and $\tau = RC$ is the time constant.

At exactly one time constant, $t = \tau$, the current becomes:

$I(\tau) = I_0 e^{-1} = \dfrac{I_0}{e}$

The initial current $I_0$ is:

$I_0 = \dfrac{6.0}{24} = 0.25 \text{ A}$

Substituting $I_0$ and the value of $e \approx 2.718$ into the equation for current:

$I(\tau) = \dfrac{0.25}{2.718} \approx 0.09 \text{ A}$

questions.q: A parallel-plate capacitor having a plate area of $40 \text{ cm}^2$ and a separation of $0.10 \text{ mm}$ between the plates is connected to a battery with an emf of $2.0 \text{ V}$ through a $16 \Omega$ resistor. Determine the electric field inside the capacitor $10 \text{ ns}$ after the connections are established.
questions.solution:
Area of the plates, $A = 40 \text{ cm}^2 = 4 \times 10^{-3} \text{ m}^2$

Separation between plates, $d = 0.10 \text{ mm} = 10^{-4} \text{ m}$

Capacitance, $C = \dfrac{\epsilon_0 A}{d} = \dfrac{8.85 \times 10^{-12} \times 4 \times 10^{-3}}{10^{-4}} = 3.54 \times 10^{-10} \text{ F}$

Time constant of the $RC$ circuit, $\tau = RC = 16 \times 3.54 \times 10^{-10} = 5.664 \times 10^{-9} \text{ s} = 5.664 \text{ ns}$

The voltage across the capacitor at time $t$ is given by:

$V(t) = V_0 \left(1 - e^{-t/\tau}\right)$

Substituting $t = 10 \text{ ns}$and $\tau = 5.664 \text{ ns}$:

$V(10 \text{ ns}) =2.0 \left(1 - e^{-\dfrac{10}{5.664}}$\right) = 2.0 \left($1 - e^{-1.765}\right)$

$V(10 $\text{ ns}) \approx$2.0 (1 - 0.171) = 2.0 $\times$0.829 = 1.658 $\text{ V}

The electric field inside the capacitor is:

$E = \dfrac{V}{d} = \dfrac{1.658}{10^{-4}} =1.658 $\times$10^4 $\text{ V/m} \approx$1.7 $\times$10^4 $\text{ V/m}

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A parallel-plate capacitor features a plate area of $20 \text{ cm}^2$, a plate separation of $1.0 \text{ mm}$, and a dielectric slab with a dielectric constant of $5.0$ filling the space between the plates. The capacitor is connected to a battery of emf $6.0 \text{ V}$ via a $100 \text{ k}\Omega$ resistor. Determine the energy of the capacitor $8.9 \mu\text{s}$ after the connections are established.
questions.solution:
The capacitance of the parallel-plate capacitor with the dielectric slab is given by:

$C = \dfrac{K \epsilon_0 A}{d}$

Substituting the given values:

$C = \dfrac{5.0 \times 8.85 \times 10^{-12} \times 20 \times 10^{-4}}{1.0 \times 10^{-3}} = 88.5 \times 10^{-12} \text{ F}$

The time constant of the RC circuit is:

$\tau = RC = (100 \times 10^3) \times (88.5 \times 10^{-12}) = 8.85 \times 10^{-6} \text{ s} = 8.85 \mu\text{s}$

The given time is $t = 8.9 \mu\text{s}$, which is approximately equal to one time constant $\tau$. The voltage across the capacitor at time $t$ is:

$V = V_0 (1 - e^{-t/\tau})$

For $t \approx \tau$:

$V \approx 6.0 (1 - e^{-1}) \approx 6.0 (1 - 0.37) = 3.78 \text{ V}$

The energy stored in the capacitor at this time is:

$U = \dfrac{1}{2} C V^2$

$U = \dfrac{1}{2} \times 88.5 \times 10^{-12} \times (3.78)^2$

$U \approx 6.3 \times 10^{-10} \text{ J}$

Answer: $6.3 \times 10^{-10} \text{ J}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A $100 \mu\text{F}$ capacitor is joined to a $24 \text{ V}$ battery via a $1.0 \text{ M}\Omega$ resistor. Which of the following best describes the qualitative graph between current and time for the first $10$ minutes?
options: A linear decrease starting from $24 \mu\text{A}$ and reaching zero.
An exponentially growing curve starting from zero and approaching $24 \mu\text{A}$.
An exponentially decaying curve starting from $24 \mu\text{A}$ and approaching zero.
questions.solution:
The given circuit is an RC charging circuit.

The time constant of the circuit is given by $\tau = RC$.

Substituting the given values:

$\tau = (1.0 \times 10^6 \Omega) \times (100 \times 10^{-6} \text{ F}) = 100 \text{ s}$

The initial current in the circuit at $t = 0$ is:

$I_0 = \dfrac{V}{R} = \dfrac{24}{1.0 \times 10^6} = 24 \mu\text{A}$

The current in an RC circuit during charging varies with time according to the equation:

$I(t) = I_0 e^{-t/\tau}$

$I(t) = 24 e^{-t/100} \mu\text{A}$

This equation represents an exponentially decaying curve. At $t = 0$, the current is $24 \mu\text{A}$, and as time progresses, it exponentially approaches zero.

For a duration of $10$ minutes ($600 \text{ s}$, which is $6\tau$), the current will have decayed to a value very close to zero. Thus, the graph is an exponentially decaying curve starting from $24 \mu\text{A}$ and approaching zero.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A $100 \mu\text{F}$ capacitor is joined to a $24 \text{ V}$ battery via a $1.0 \text{ M}\Omega$ resistor. Which of the following best describes the qualitative graph between charge and time for the first $10$ minutes?
options: An exponentially decaying curve starting from $2400 \mu\text{C}$ and approaching zero.
A linear increase starting from zero and reaching $2400 \mu\text{C}$.
An exponentially growing curve starting from zero and approaching $2400 \mu\text{C}$.
questions.solution:
The time constant of the $RC$ circuit is given by $\tau = RC = (1.0 \times 10^6 \Omega)(100 \times 10^{-6} \text{ F}) = 100 \text{ s}$.

The maximum steady-state charge on the capacitor is $Q_0 = CV = (100 \mu\text{F})(24 \text{ V}) = 2400 \mu\text{C}$.

The equation for the charge on a charging capacitor as a function of time is $q(t) = Q_0 (1 - e^{-t/\tau})$.

This equation represents an exponentially growing curve that starts from zero at $t = 0$ and asymptotically approaches the maximum charge $Q_0 = 2400 \mu\text{C}$.

Since the given time interval is $10 \text{ minutes} = 600 \text{ s} = 6\tau$, the capacitor will be nearly fully charged by the end of this period. Thus, the graph is an exponentially growing curve starting from zero and approaching $2400 \mu\text{C}$.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: How many time constants will elapse before the current in a charging RC circuit decreases to half of its initial value? Answer the same question for a discharging RC circuit.
questions.solution:
For a charging RC circuit, the current at any time $t$ is given by $i = i_0 e^{-t/\tau}$, where $\tau = RC$ is the time constant and $i_0$ is the initial current.

We are given that the current decreases to half of its initial value, so $i = \dfrac{i_0}{2}$.

$\dfrac{i_0}{2} = i_0 e^{-t/\tau}$

$e^{t/\tau} = 2$

$\dfrac{t}{\tau} = \ln 2 \approx 0.693$

$t \approx 0.69 \tau$

For a discharging RC circuit, the current at any time $t$ is also given by $i = i_0 e^{-t/\tau}$.

Similarly, for the current to decrease to half of its initial value, $i = \dfrac{i_0}{2}$.

$\dfrac{i_0}{2} = i_0 e^{-t/\tau}$

$e^{t/\tau} = 2$

$\dfrac{t}{\tau} = \ln 2 \approx 0.693$

$t \approx 0.69 \tau$

Thus, in both cases, $0.69$ time constants will elapse.
