questions.q: In a discharging RC circuit, how many time constants must elapse for the charge on a capacitor to decrease to $0.1\%$ of its maximum value?
questions.solution:
The charge on a discharging capacitor at any time $t$ is given by the equation:

$q = q_{0} e^{-t/\tau}$

where $q_{0}$ is the maximum initial charge and $\tau$ is the time constant of the circuit.

Given that the charge decreases to $0.1\%$ of its maximum value:

$q = 0.1\% \text{ of } q_{0} = \dfrac{0.1}{100} q_{0} = 10^{-3} q_{0}$

Substituting this into the discharging equation:

$10^{-3} q_{0} = q_{0} e^{-t/\tau}$

$e^{-t/\tau} = 10^{-3}$

Taking the natural logarithm on both sides:

$\dfrac{-t}{\tau} = \ln(10^{-3})$

$\dfrac{-t}{\tau} = -3 \ln(10)$

Using the value $\ln(10) \approx 2.303$:

$t = 3 \times 2.303 \tau$

$t \approx 6.9 \tau$

Thus, $6.9$ time constants must elapse.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: In a charging RC circuit, determine the number of time constants that will elapse before the energy stored in the capacitor attains half of its equilibrium value.
questions.solution:
The energy stored in a capacitor at any time $t$ is given by $U = \dfrac{q^2}{2C}$, where $q$ is the charge on the capacitor at time $t$.

The maximum (equilibrium) energy stored in the capacitor is $U_0 = \dfrac{q_0^2}{2C}$, where $q_0$ is the maximum charge.

Given that the energy attains half of its equilibrium value:

$U = \dfrac{U_0}{2}$

$\dfrac{q^2}{2C} = \dfrac{1}{2} \dfrac{q_0^2}{2C}$

$q = \dfrac{q_0}{\sqrt{2}}$

For a charging RC circuit, the charge as a function of time is:

$q = q_0(1 - e^{-t/\tau})$

Substituting $q = \dfrac{q_0}{\sqrt{2}}$:

$\dfrac{q_0}{\sqrt{2}} = q_0(1 - e^{-t/\tau})$

$1 - e^{-t/\tau} = \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{2}}$

$e^{-t/\tau} = 1 - \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{2}} = \dfrac{\sqrt{2}-1}{\sqrt{2}}$

$e^{t/\tau} = \dfrac{\sqrt{2}}{\sqrt{2}-1} = \sqrt{2}(\sqrt{2}+1) = 2 + \sqrt{2}$

Taking the natural logarithm on both sides:

$\dfrac{t}{\tau} = \ln(2 + \sqrt{2})$

Since $\sqrt{2} \approx 1.414$:

$\dfrac{t}{\tau} = \ln(3.414) \approx 1.228 \approx 1.23$

Thus, the number of time constants that will elapse is approximately $1.23$.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: In an RC circuit, how many time constants must elapse before the power delivered by the battery decreases to half of its maximum value?
questions.solution:
The power delivered by the battery in an RC circuit is given by $P = VI$, where $V$ is the constant voltage of the battery and $I$ is the current.

The current in a charging RC circuit as a function of time is $I = I_0 e^{-t/\tau}$, where $I_0$ is the maximum current at $t = 0$ and $\tau$ is the time constant.

Substituting the expression for current, the power delivered by the battery is:

$P = V I_0 e^{-t/\tau} = P_{\max} e^{-t/\tau}$

We need to find the time $t$ when the power decreases to half of its maximum value, so $P = \dfrac{P_{\max}}{2}$.

$\dfrac{P_{\max}}{2} = P_{\max} e^{-t/\tau}$

$e^{-t/\tau} = \dfrac{1}{2}$

Taking the natural logarithm on both sides:

$\dfrac{t}{\tau} = \ln(2)$

$t = \tau \ln(2) \approx 0.693 \tau$

Thus, approximately $0.69$ time constants must elapse.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: At $t = 0$, a capacitor having capacitance $C$ is connected through a resistance $R$ to a battery of emf $\mathcal{E}$. Determine the maximum rate of energy storage in the capacitor, and find the time at which this maximum rate is reached.
questions.solution:
The charge on the capacitor at time $t$ is given by $q = C\mathcal{E}(1 - e^{-t/RC})$.

The current in the circuit is $i = \dfrac{dq}{dt} = \dfrac{\mathcal{E}}{R} e^{-t/RC}$.

The rate of energy storage in the capacitor is $P = \dfrac{dU}{dt} = \dfrac{d}{dt} \left( \dfrac{q^2}{2C} \right) = \dfrac{q}{C} i$.

Substituting the expressions for $q$ and $i$ gives:

$P = \dfrac{C\mathcal{E}(1 - e^{-t/RC})}{C} \dfrac{\mathcal{E}}{R} e^{-t/RC} = \dfrac{\mathcal{E}^2}{R} (e^{-t/RC} - e^{-2t/RC})$.

To find the maximum rate of energy storage, let $x = e^{-t/RC}$. Then $P = \dfrac{\mathcal{E}^2}{R} (x - x^2)$.

For maximum $P$, $\dfrac{dP}{dx} = 0 \Rightarrow 1 - 2x = 0 \Rightarrow x = \dfrac{1}{2}$.

Thus, $e^{-t/RC} = \dfrac{1}{2} \Rightarrow t = CR \ln 2$.

The maximum rate of energy storage is $P_\max = \dfrac{\mathcal{E}^2}{R} \left( \dfrac{1}{2} - \dfrac{1}{4} \right) = \dfrac{\mathcal{E}^2}{4R}$.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: Through resistanceless leads, a capacitor of capacitance $12.0 \mu\text{F}$ is connected to a battery of emf $6.00 \text{ V}$ and internal resistance $1.00 \Omega$. Determine the current in the circuit $12.0 \mu\text{s}$ after the connections are made.
questions.solution:
The time constant of the RC circuit is given by $\tau = RC$.

Substituting the given values:
$\tau = 1.00 \times 12.0 \times 10^{-6} = 12.0 \mu\text{s}$

The current in the circuit during the charging of a capacitor is given by:
$I = I_0 e^{-t/\tau}$

The initial current $I_0$ is:
$I_0 = \dfrac{E}{R} = \dfrac{6.00}{1.00} = 6.00 \text{ A}$

At $t = 12.0 \mu\text{s}$, we have $t = \tau$. Substituting this into the current equation:
$I = 6.00 \times e^{-1} = \dfrac{6.00}{e}$

Using $e \approx 2.718$:
$I = \dfrac{6.00}{2.718} \approx 2.21 \text{ A}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: Through resistanceless leads, a capacitor of capacitance $12.0 \mu\text{F}$ is connected to a battery of emf $6.00 \text{ V}$ and internal resistance $1.00 \Omega$. Determine the power delivered by the battery $12.0 \mu\text{s}$ after the connections are made.
questions.solution:
The time constant of the RC circuit is given by:

$\tau = RC = 1.00 \times 12.0 \times 10^{-6} = 12.0 \mu\text{s}$

The current in the circuit as a function of time is:

$I(t) = \dfrac{E}{R} e^{-t/\tau}$

At $t = 12.0 \mu\text{s}$, we have $t = \tau$. Substituting the values:

$I = \dfrac{6.00}{1.00} e^{-1} = \dfrac{6.00}{e} \approx 2.207 \text{ A}$

The total power delivered by the battery is the power supplied by its emf, which is given by:

$P = EI$

$P = 6.00 \times 2.207 \approx 13.24 \text{ W}$

Rounding to three significant figures, the power delivered is $13.2 \text{ W}$.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: Through resistanceless leads, a capacitor of capacitance $12.0 \mu\text{F}$ is connected to a battery of emf $6.00 \text{ V}$ and internal resistance $1.00 \Omega$. Determine the power dissipated as heat $12.0 \mu\text{s}$ after the connections are made.
questions.solution:
The time constant of the RC circuit is given by $\tau = RC$.

Substituting the given values, $\tau = (1.00 \Omega) \times (12.0 \mu\text{F}) = 12.0 \mu\text{s}$.

The current in the circuit during charging is given by $I(t) = \dfrac{V}{R} e^{-t/\tau}$.

At $t = 12.0 \mu\text{s}$, we have $t = \tau$.

$I = \dfrac{6.00}{1.00} e^{-1} = \dfrac{6.00}{e} \text{ A}$.

The power dissipated as heat in the internal resistance is $P = I^2 R$.

$P = \left( \dfrac{6.00}{e} \right)^2 \times 1.00 = \dfrac{36.0}{e^2} \text{ W}$.

Using $e \approx 2.718$, we get $P \approx \dfrac{36.0}{7.389} \approx 4.87 \text{ W}$.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: Through resistanceless leads, a capacitor of capacitance $12.0 \mu\text{F}$ is connected to a battery of emf $6.00 \text{ V}$ and internal resistance $1.00 \Omega$. Determine the rate at which the energy stored in the capacitor is increasing $12.0 \mu\text{s}$ after the connections are made.
questions.solution:
The energy stored in a capacitor is given by $U = \dfrac{q^2}{2C}$.

The rate at which the energy is increasing is $\dfrac{dU}{dt} = \dfrac{q}{C} \dfrac{dq}{dt} = V_c I$.

For an RC circuit during charging, the voltage across the capacitor and the current are given by:

$V_c = E(1 - e^{-t/RC})$

$I = \dfrac{E}{R} e^{-t/RC}$

The time constant of the circuit is $\tau = RC = (1.00 \Omega)(12.0 \mu\text{F}) = 12.0 \mu\text{s}$.

At the given time $t = 12.0 \mu\text{s}$, we have $t = \tau$. Substituting this into the equations:

$V_c = E(1 - e^{-1})$

$I = \dfrac{E}{R} e^{-1}$

The rate of increase of energy is:

$\dfrac{dU}{dt} = E(1 - e^{-1}) \times \dfrac{E}{R} e^{-1} = \dfrac{E^2}{R} (e^{-1} - e^{-2})$

Substituting the given values $E = 6.00 \text{ V}$ and $R = 1.00 \Omega$:

$\dfrac{dU}{dt} = \dfrac{(6.00)^2}{1.00} $\$left(\dfrac{1}{e} - \dfrac{1}{e^2}\right)

Using $e \approx 2.718$:

\dfrac{dU}{dt} =$36.0 \times (0.3679 - 0.1353) = 36.0 \times 0.2326 = 8.37 \text{ W}$.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A capacitance $C$ charged to a potential difference $V$ is discharged by connecting its plates across a resistance $R$. Determine the heat dissipated during one time constant after the connections are established. (This can be evaluated by computing $\int i^2 R \, dt$ or by assessing the reduction in the energy stored within the capacitor.)
questions.solution:
The initial energy stored in the capacitor is $U_i = \dfrac{1}{2}CV^2$.

During the discharging of a capacitor, the voltage across it at any time $t$ is given by $V(t) = V e^{-t/RC}$.

After one time constant $t = RC$, the voltage becomes $V(RC) = V e^{-1} = \dfrac{V}{e}$.

The energy stored in the capacitor at this time is $U_f = \dfrac{1}{2}C \left(\dfrac{V}{e}\right)^2 = $\dfrac{1}{2}$CV^2 \left(\dfrac{1}{e^2}\right).

By conservation of energy, the heat dissipated across the resistor is equal to the loss in the electrical potential energy of the capacitor.

$H = U_i - U_f = $\dfrac{1}{2}$CV^2 - $\dfrac{1}{2}$CV^2 \left(\dfrac{1}{e^2}\right) = \dfrac{1}{2}CV^2 \left(1 - \dfrac{1}{e^2}\right)$.$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A parallel-plate capacitor is filled with a dielectric material having resistivity $\rho$ and dielectric constant $K$. The capacitor is charged and disconnected from the charging source. It is then slowly discharged through the dielectric. Determine the time constant of the discharge, noting that it is independent of geometrical parameters such as the separation between the plates or the plate area.
questions.solution:
The capacitance of a parallel-plate capacitor filled with a dielectric of constant $K$ is given by:

$C = \dfrac{K \varepsilon_0 A}{d}$

where $A$ is the area of the plates and $d$ is the separation between them.

The resistance of the dielectric material between the plates is given by:

$R = \dfrac{\rho d}{A}$

where $\rho$ is the resistivity of the material.

The time constant $\tau$ for the discharge of the capacitor through the dielectric is the product of its resistance and capacitance:

$\tau = R C$

Substituting the expressions for $R$ and $C$, we get:

$\tau = \left( \dfrac{\rho d}{A} \right) \left( $\dfrac{K \varepsilon_0 A}{d} \right)

$\tau = \varepsilon_0 \rho K$

The time constant is independent of the geometrical parameters $A$ and $d$.

questions.q: Determine the charge on each capacitor $0.20\ \text{ms}$ after closing switch $S$, as shown in the figure.
questions.solution:
The two capacitors are connected in parallel. Their equivalent capacitance is:

$C_{eq} = 2.0\ \mu\text{F} + 2.0\ \mu\text{F} = 4.0\ \mu\text{F}$

The time constant of the circuit is:

$\tau = R C_{eq} = 25\ \Omega \times 4.0 \times 10^{-6}\ \text{F} = 100 \times 10^{-6}\ \text{s} = 0.10\ \text{ms}$

The maximum total charge on the equivalent capacitor is:

$Q_{max} = C_{eq} V = 4.0\ \mu\text{F} \times 6.0\ \text{V} = 24.0\ \mu\text{C}$

The total charge at time $t = 0.20\ \text{ms}$ is given by:

$Q(t) = Q_{max} (1 - e^{-t/\tau})$

$Q(0.20\ \text{ms}) = 24.0 (1 - e^{-0.20/0.10}) = 24.0 (1 - e^{-2})$

Using $e^{-2} \approx 0.1353$:

$Q = 24.0 (1 - 0.1353) = 24.0 \times 0.8647 \approx 20.75\ \mu\text{C}$

Since the two identical capacitors are in parallel, they share the total charge equally. The charge on each capacitor is:

$q = \dfrac{Q}{2} = \dfrac{20.75}{2} \approx 10.37\ \mu\text{C}$

questions.q: By evaluating $\int i^2 R \, dt$, determine how the energy dissipated as heat relates to the energy stored in the capacitor when it is charged by connecting it to a battery via a resistor.
options: The energy dissipated as heat is zero.
The energy dissipated as heat is twice the energy stored in the capacitor.
The energy dissipated as heat is half the energy stored in the capacitor.
The energy dissipated as heat equals the energy stored in the capacitor.
questions.solution:
Let the capacitance be $C$, resistance be $R$, and the voltage of the battery be $V$.

The current in the circuit at any time $t$ during charging is given by:
$i = \dfrac{V}{R} e^{-t/RC}$

The energy dissipated as heat across the resistor is:
$H = \int_{0}^{\infty} i^2 R \, dt$

Substituting the expression for $i$:
$H = \int_{0}^{\infty} \left( \dfrac{V}{R} e^{-t/RC} \right)^2 R \, dt$

$H = \dfrac{V^2}{R} \int_{0}^{\infty} e^{-2t/RC} \, dt$

$H = \dfrac{V^2}{R} \left[ \dfrac{e^{-2t/RC}}{-2/RC} \right]_{0}^{\infty}$

$H = \dfrac{V^2}{R} \left( 0 - \left( $-\dfrac{RC}{2} \right) \right)

$H = $\dfrac{1}{2}$C V^2$

The energy stored in the capacitor when fully charged is:
$U = $\dfrac{1}{2}$C V^2$

Thus, the energy dissipated as heat is equal to the energy stored in the capacitor.

questions.q: The switch $S$ illustrated in the figure is kept closed for a long duration and is subsequently opened at $t = 0$. Determine the current in the middle $10\ \Omega$ resistor at $t = 1.0\ \text{ms}$.
questions.solution:
When the switch $S$ is closed for a long time, the circuit reaches a steady state. In this state, the capacitor acts as an open circuit and no current flows through its branch.

The steady current $I$ flows through the outer loop containing the $12\ \text{V}$ battery and the two $10\ \Omega$ resistors in series:
$I = \dfrac{12}{10 + 10} = 0.6\ \text{A}$

The potential difference across the middle $10\ \Omega$ resistor is:
$V_0 = I \times 10 = 0.6 \times 10 = 6\ \text{V}$
Since the capacitor is in parallel with this resistor, the initial voltage across the capacitor is $V_0 = 6\ \text{V}$.

When the switch $S$ is opened at $t = 0$, the battery and the bottom resistor are disconnected. The capacitor now discharges through the middle $10\ \Omega$ resistor.

The time constant $\tau$ of this discharging circuit is:
$\tau = RC = 10 \times 25 \times 10^{-6} = 250\ \mu\text{s} = 0.25\ \text{ms}$

The current $i(t)$ in the discharging circuit at time $t$ is given by:
$i(t) = \dfrac{V_0}{R} e^{-t/\tau}$

Substituting $t = 1.0\ \text{ms}$:
$i(1.0\ \text{ms}) = \dfrac{6}{10} e^{-1.0/0.25} = 0.6 e^{-4}$

Using the value $e^{-4} \approx 0.0183$:
$i(1.0\ \text{ms}) \approx 0.6 \times 0.0183 = 0.01098\ \text{A} \approx 0.011\ \text{A}$

questions.q: A capacitor with a capacitance of $100\mu\text{F}$ is connected for $4.0\text{ s}$ across a $6.0\text{ V}$ battery through a $20\text{ k}\Omega$ resistance. Following this, the battery is replaced by a thick wire. Determine the charge on the capacitor $4.0\text{ s}$ after disconnecting the battery.
questions.solution:
Time constant of the circuit is given by:

$\tau = RC = (20 \times 10^{3}) \times (100 \times 10^{-6}) = 2.0\text{ s}$

Maximum charge on the capacitor is:

$Q_{0} = CV = (100\mu\text{F}) \times (6.0\text{ V}) = 600\mu\text{C}$

During the charging phase for $t_{1} = 4.0\text{ s}$, the charge on the capacitor is:

$Q_{1} = Q_{0}(1 - e^{-t_{1}/\tau}) = Q_{0}(1 - e^{-4.0/2.0}) = Q_{0}(1 - e^{-2})$

When the battery is replaced by a thick wire, the capacitor discharges through the same resistor. The charge after discharging for $t_{2} = 4.0\text{ s}$ is:

$Q_{2} = Q_{1}e^{-t_{2}/\tau} = Q_{1}e^{-4.0/2.0} = Q_{1}e^{-2}$

Substituting the value of $Q_{1}$:

$Q_{2} = Q_{0}(1 - e^{-2})e^{-2} = Q_{0}(e^{-2} - e^{-4})$

Using $e^{-2} \approx 0.1353$ and $e^{-4} \approx 0.0183$:

$Q_{2} = 600(0.1353 - 0.0183) = 600(0.117) = 70.2\mu\text{C}$

The charge on the capacitor is approximately $70\mu\text{C}$.

questions.q: In the circuit depicted in the figure, the capacitors are initially uncharged. If the switch is closed at $t = 0$, determine the charge on the capacitor $C_1$ as a function of time $t$.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A capacitor having capacitance $C$ is given an initial charge $Q$. At time $t = 0$, it is connected across an uncharged capacitor of the same capacitance via a resistance $R$. Determine the charge accumulated on the second capacitor as a function of time.
questions.solution:
Let $q_1$ and $q_2$ be the charges on the first and second capacitors at time $t$.

By conservation of charge, $q_1 + q_2 = Q$.

Applying Kirchhoff's voltage law in the circuit:

$\dfrac{q_1}{C} - iR - \dfrac{q_2}{C} = 0$

Since $i = \dfrac{dq_2}{dt}$ and $q_1 = Q - q_2$, we have:

$\dfrac{Q - q_2}{C} - \dfrac{q_2}{C} = R \dfrac{dq_2}{dt}$

$\dfrac{Q - 2q_2}{C} = R \dfrac{dq_2}{dt}$

$\dfrac{dq_2}{Q - 2q_2} = \dfrac{dt}{RC}$

Integrating both sides with limits $q_2 = 0$ at $t = 0$ to $q_2$ at time $t$:

$\int_{0}^{q_2} \dfrac{dq_2}{Q - 2q_2} = \int_{0}^{t} \dfrac{dt}{RC}$

$-\dfrac{1}{2} \ln \left( \dfrac{Q - 2q_2}{Q} \right) = \dfrac{t}{RC}$

$\ln \left( \dfrac{Q - 2q_2}{Q} \right) = -\dfrac{2t}{RC}$

$Q - 2q_2 = Q e^{-2t/RC}$

$q_2 = \dfrac{Q}{2}(1 - e^{-2t/RC})$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A capacitor having capacitance $C$ is initially provided with a charge $Q$. At $t = 0$, it is linked to an ideal battery of emf $\mathcal{E}$ via a resistance $R$. Determine the charge on the capacitor at time $t$.
questions.solution:
Applying Kirchhoff's loop rule for the circuit at time $t$:

$\mathcal{E} - iR - \dfrac{q}{C} = 0$

Substituting $i = \dfrac{dq}{dt}$:

$R \dfrac{dq}{dt} = \mathcal{E} - \dfrac{q}{C} = \dfrac{C\mathcal{E} - q}{C}$

Rearranging and integrating with the initial condition $q(0) = Q$:

$\int_Q^{q} \dfrac{dq}{C\mathcal{E} - q} = \int_{0}^{t} \dfrac{dt}{RC}$

$[-\ln(C\mathcal{E} - q)]_Q^{q} = \dfrac{t}{RC}$

$\ln\left(\dfrac{C\mathcal{E} - q}{C\mathcal{E} - Q}\right) = -\dfrac{t}{RC}$

$C\mathcal{E} - q = (C\mathcal{E} - Q) e^{-\dfrac{t}{RC}}$

$q = C\mathcal{E}\left(1 - e^{-\dfrac{t}{RC}}\right) + Q e^{-\dfrac{t}{RC}}$
